XI. Wise Conduct within the Household (5:15–6:9)

A. Introduction: Wisdom and the Life Filled in the Spirit (5:15–20)

B. Submission in the Believing Household (5:21–6:9)


A. Introduction: Wisdom and the Life Filled in the Spirit (5:15–20)

Paul begins his new body of positive advice by sounding a cautionary note. “The days are evil” (5:16; cf. 2:2), and therefore it is easy even for believers to be “wave-tossed and blown around by every wind of teaching, by human trickery, by cunning, in the service of the system of error” (4:14; cf. 6:11, 16). It is necessary, therefore, for believers to walk carefully (5:15), with wisdom (5:15), with understanding (5:17), and with lives that are fulfilled because they are lived in the sphere marked out by God’s Spirit (5:18). As a result of living this way, the corporate worship of believers will include instructional singing to one another and to the Lord (5:19) and thanksgiving to God for all that he has done for believers through the Lord Jesus Christ (5:20).

The section can be divided into two parts. The first part (5:15–18) continues the contrast between the unbelieving and believing way of life that has characterized 5:3–14 but quickly gives way, in the second part (5:19–20), to a positive description of Christian worship. This second section lays the groundwork for the household code that follows in two ways: it shifts the readers’ attention to the household since early Christian worship took place in houses, and it introduces a sustained positive tone that will continue, with only brief negative interruptions (5:29; 6:4, 6, 9), to the end of the household code.



Exegesis and Exposition

15Watch carefully therefore how you walk, not as unwise but as wise people, 16by redeeming the time, because the days are evil. 17Because of this, do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is. 18Do not get drunk with wine, in which is debauchery, but be filled in the Spirit, 19speaking among yourselves ⌜with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs⌝, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord, 20giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, ⌜who is also Father⌝.

[5:15–16] Paul now issues a warning to his readers to walk carefully and wisely, and this warning arises out of what he has said in the previous section (οὖν, oun, therefore). Paul’s readers should not participate in the activities of “the sons of disobedience” (5:6, 11) and should not be deceived by false teachers claiming otherwise (5:6). “Therefore,” he says, “watch carefully how you walk.”[1] The emphasis may fall on the special care with which Paul’s readers should walk because he is aware of the efforts of some people to deceive believers with the idea that those engaged in sexual immorality and greed will come to no harm (5:6). He is aware that his readers are engaged in a battle of the mind in which “human trickery” and “cunning” make false teaching look attractive (4:14), and the futile and darkened understanding of unbelieving Gentiles, which his readers once shared, can still pose a threat (4:17–19). His readers must walk through a mental minefield of ideas that, if they are not careful, will lead them to despair, shame, and the wrath of God (4:19; 5:6, 12). Therefore they should carefully watch their step.

Paul describes the care they should exercise in their behavior with two phrases. First, they should walk “not as unwise [ἄσοφοι, asophoi] but as wise [σοφοί, sophoi] people.” So far in the letter the noun “wisdom” (σοφία, sophia) has referred either to God’s wisdom (1:8; 3:10) or to the wisdom that God gives about his purposes for his people and for the universe (1:17). Here, however, the adjective “wise” describes the person who is skilled in “finding what is pleasing to the Lord” (5:10; cf. Rom. 16:19; James 3:13), just as the artisan is skilled in the practice of a particular craft.[2] Paul will repeat this thought in different terms in 5:17.

Second, they should also walk carefully “by redeeming the time” (ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν, exagorazomenoi ton kairon). The verb ἐξαγοράζω (exagorazō) can mean simply “buy” or “buy up,” as when Nebuchadnezzar tells the dream interpreters of Babylon that, by asking him to tell them the content of the dream before they tell him its meaning, they are simply trying to “buy time” (Dan. 2:8 NETS). The verb can also mean to “buy” something “out” or “away” from some condition or situation, such as the law or its curse (Gal. 3:13; 4:5; Robinson 1904: 202; MHT 2:309). In the middle voice, it can refer to buying a slave’s freedom with a dash of self-interest thrown in (Diodorus Siculus, Biblio. hist. 36.2a).[3] Here, then, Paul instructs his readers to “buy the time” away from (ἐκ, ek) something that has a grip on it.

What has a grip on the present time? He explains in the phrase “the days are evil.” By this expression Paul means what he has already said in 2:2, that “the Course [αἰών, aiōn] of this world” is aligned with the devil (2:2; cf. 6:12–13). His readers are to buy the present time out of its slavery to evil and to use it instead in ways that are “pleasing to the Lord” (5:10).[4] Since Paul will later speak of the present time in the singular as “the evil day” (6:13), the plural “days” is probably thoughtfully chosen here, and it fits well with the use of καιρός (kairos), which here means “a moment or period as especially appropriate” (BDAG 497). The business of buying time out of its slavery to evil takes place day by day, moment by moment, in the practical decisions of everyday life.

[5:17] Because the days are evil, Paul says, his readers should not be foolish but understand the Lord’s will. The phrase διὰ τοῦτο (dia touto, because of this) refers to the last clause of 5:16: the days are evil. Just as evil times supply the reason for redeeming the time (ὅτι, hoti, because), so they supply the reason (διὰ τοῦτο) for not being foolish but understanding the Lord’s will. This means that redeeming the time and understanding the Lord’s will stand parallel to and define each other. To understand (συνίημι, syniēmi) the Lord’s will, and presumably to act on it, is to buy the present “time” out of its slavery to evil. The concept of understanding “what the will of the Lord is” is similar to the idea in 5:10 of “trying to find out what is pleasing to the Lord,” and the whole thought is similar to the famous statement at the beginning of Proverbs, “The fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, and good understanding [σύνεσις, synesis] belongs to all who practice it” (1:7 LXX, my trans.). Paul probably considers this a matter both of following the guidelines he has supplied in 4:25–5:14 and 5:21–6:20 and of using the renewed mind (4:23; cf. 1:17–18a) that has come through the Spirit at conversion (1:13) to discern how one should act in various complex ethical situations.

Paul believed that his readers lived in a world over which the devil and other evil spiritual powers had considerable influence (2:2; 6:12–13). He also believed that human beings were by nature “children of wrath” and only too willing to devote their thoughts to doing the desires of the flesh (2:3). In a world of such exterior and interior evil forces, it was especially critical to know the Lord’s will and to make wise decisions about what it involved in one’s day-to-day existence.

[5:18] The prohibition μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ (mē methyskesthe oinō, do not get drunk with wine), together with its contrasting command to be filled with the Spirit, has seemed jarring and off-topic to a number of interpreters. Paul has been speaking in general terms of acting wisely or unwisely, and so a specific admonition to avoid drunkenness seems out of place. What can account for this?

Some interpreters have proposed that this specific admonition was prompted by a correspondingly specific problem among the letter’s readers. One group of interpreters believes that the cult of Dionysus, which involved ritual drunkenness and frenzied behavior, has influenced the readers’ behavior. In response, the letter’s author urges his readers to understand the incompatibility of Christian worship, with its Spirit-filled utterances (5:19), and the wine-induced behavior of Bacchic rites (e.g., Preisker, TDNT 4:548). Other interpreters suggest that the Christian “agape feast” (Jude 12; 2 Pet. 2:13) has for the letter’s readers become debauched by pagan practices of feasting (De Wette 1843: 149; Gnilka 1971: 269). Still others wonder whether the stress of living in “evil days” (5:16), or a libertine morality prompted by an overrealized eschatology, has led to drunkenness (Barth 1974: 581).

It is much more likely, however, that the author is simply reflecting a common concern with drunkenness in the ancient literature of moral exhortation. In his ethical instruction to Demonicus, for example, Isocrates warns Demonicus about becoming intoxicated at drinking parties: “For when the mind is impaired by wine, it is like chariots which have lost their drivers. . . . The soul stumbles again and again when the intellect is impaired” (Isocrates, Demon. 32, trans. Norlin 1928–29; cf. W. Wilson 2005: 114). In a Hellenistic Jewish context, the Greek translation of Proverbs 20:1 (cf. 23:19–21) warns that whoever gets mixed up with intemperate wine and outrageous drunkenness is not wise (σοφός, sophos), and later uses precisely the phrase that appears here in Ephesians to warn μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ (Prov. 23:31 LXX). The same phrase resurfaces in T. Jud. 14.1, again with a reference to the impact of wine on the mind’s ability to make good ethical decisions: “Do not be drunk with wine, because wine perverts the mind from truth, arouses the impulses of desire, and leads the eyes into the path of error” (OTP 1:799). It thus seems to have been natural in literature that counseled people to use good ethical judgment also to counsel them to avoid heavy drinking, since drunkenness could seriously damage one’s ability to make wise decisions about how to behave (cf. Darko 2008: 61–62).

If a specific cultural occasion where this might occur was in Paul’s mind when he wrote this admonition, it may well have been the sort of lavish banqueting that sometimes gave rise to obscene speech, nonsensical babbling, and sexually suggestive humor (see the comments on 5:4 above; cf. Eadie 1883: 396–97; Gosnell 1993). This context would at least fit well with Paul’s further comment that connects drunkenness with ἀσωτία (asōtia, debauchery), a term that “is very often associated with drinking binges during festivals” (Spicq, TLNT 1:220, citing 2 Macc. 6:4; Athenaeus, Deipn. 4.59–67; cf. 1 Pet. 4:4; Rom. 13:13).

Instead, Paul urges his readers, πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι (plērousthe en pneumati, be filled in the Spirit). As the five adverbial participles that qualify this phrase show, this positive command, and not the prohibition of drunkenness, is where Paul’s emphasis lies (Fee 1994: 720). Since so much in the rest of the paragraph is built upon it syntactically, the phrase merits close scrutiny. Two questions are particularly important.

First, what does the verb’s present tense signify? Does Paul want to say that his readers should be continually filled (Fee 1994: 720; Hoehner 2002: 704), or does the tense carry no special significance here (Best 1998: 508)? Best (1998: 508) is probably correct that the present-tense imperatives in the verse (μὴ μεθύσκεσθε, πληροῦσθε) carry no more of a continuous nuance than the present imperatives that appear from 4:25 up to this point. When Paul says, for example, that his readers should speak the truth, not let the sun set on their anger, steal no longer, and let no rotten speech come from their mouth, he is not especially emphasizing the ongoing nature of these actions, and similarly there is probably no special stress on ceasing drunkenness or continuous filling here.

Second, what does the preposition ἐν mean in this phrase? Does Paul want his readers to be filled “with” the Spirit, meaning that the Spirit is the content that fills them (e.g., Best 1998: 508)? Does he want them to be filled “by” the Spirit, in the sense that the Spirit is the means by which their filling takes place (e.g., Robinson 1904: 204; Wallace 1996: 375; O’Brien 1999: 391–92; Hoehner 2002: 704)? Does he want them to be filled “in” either the human spirit (e.g., Origen [Heine 2002: 227]; Abbott 1897: 162; Westcott 1906: 81) or the Holy Spirit (Heil 2007b: 506–16), referring to the sphere in which their filling should take place? Some interpreters believe that a combination of these ideas is present: the Spirit is both the sphere in which one is filled and the content with which one is filled (Alford 1857: 130), or the Spirit is both the sphere in which one is filled and the means by which the filling takes place (Ellicott 1859: 124), or the Spirit is both the means and the content of the filling (Lincoln 1990: 344; Schnackenburg 1991: 237).

We can quickly rule out several of these options. As most interpreters now recognize, Paul probably does not refer to the human spirit here since every other time he uses the phrase ἐν πνεύματι in Ephesians, it refers to God’s Spirit (2:22; 3:5; 6:18). In addition, the explanations that find a combination of meanings in the preposition should come into play only if a single meaning makes no sense, yet “with,” “by,” and “in” each provides a perfectly intelligible rendering of the phrase (cf. Hoehner 2002: 703–4).

If we seek help in the analogy that Paul seems to imply between the controlling influence of wine and the controlling influence of the Spirit, then “with” seems to be the most likely reading. Just as the drunken person is full of, and controlled by, wine, so the believer should be full of, and directed by, the Spirit.

Normally, however, the verb πληρόω (plēroō, fill) expresses the content of the filling with a genitive-case noun, just as the verb “fill” does in English: “The whole earth will be full [πληρωθήσεται, plērōthēsetai] of his glory [δόξης, doxēs]!” (Ps. 71:19 LXX, my trans. [72:19 MT, Eng.]).[5] Moreover, Paul seems to distinguish between the relationship of wine to drunkenness and the relationship of the Spirit to fullness by inserting the preposition ἐν into the qualifying phrase: “do not be drunk οἴνῳ,” he says, but “be filled ἐν πνεύματι.”

This leaves either “by the Spirit” or “in the Spirit” as the most likely options. If “by the Spirit” is correct, then the language would match fairly neatly Paul’s talk elsewhere of walking “by the Spirit” (πνεύματι, pneumati; Gal. 5:16; cf. 5:25b) or “according to the Spirit” (κατὰ πνεῦμα, kata pneuma; Rom. 8:4; Fee 1994: 721). In these passages, the Spirit dwells in believers (Rom. 8:9; cf. Gal. 5:25a; Eph. 1:13; 2:22), but believers must cooperate with the Spirit’s indwelling if they are to live in ways that are pleasing to the Lord and consistent with his will (Rom. 8:8; cf. Gal. 5:17–25; Eph. 5:10, 17). So here, Paul would be saying that believers should cooperate with the Spirit in their own filling, with the content of that filling left undefined. This explanation is not entirely satisfying, however, since Paul speaks here not of “living” or “walking” but of “being filled,” and this takes place not πνεύματι or κατὰ πνεῦμα but ἐν πνεύματι.

For this reason, Heil’s argument (2007b: 507) is probably correct that “the preposition ‘in’ (ἐν) refers to being within the dynamic realm or sphere established and characterized by having been given the Spirit.” Three elements of Heil’s case are particularly compelling. First, he argues that everywhere else Paul uses the verb πληρόω in Ephesians (1:23; 3:19; 4:10), Christ is the one who fills or the one by whom the filling takes place (Heil 2007b: 506–7). It is possible to quibble with Heil over whether God or Christ stands behind the passive forms of πληρόω in 1:23 and 3:19,﻿[6] but he is correct that in none of the other three instances does the Spirit give fullness. This, as he says, makes it unlikely that the Spirit is the source or agent of the fullness here.

Second, he observes that when Paul qualifies drunkenness with the phrase ἐν ᾧ ἐστιν ἀσωτία (en hō estin asōtia, in which is debauchery), Paul is explaining the sphere in which drunkenness takes place. Since this phrase stands parallel to the phrase ἐν πνεύματι, it is likely that ἐν πνεύματι also describes the realm or sphere of its verb. Wine and the Spirit do not parallel each other as the instruments of drunkenness and filling. Instead, drunkenness takes place in the realm of debauchery, and the believer’s filling takes place in the realm of the Spirit (Heil 2007b: 514–15).

Third, this understanding of the phrase is consistent with, and may be another aspect of, Paul’s understanding of existence “in Christ” in Ephesians (e.g., 1:1, 3, 6, 7, 11, 13, 15; 2:6, 10, 13; 3:6; 4:32). Just as believers live in “the dynamic realm or sphere” of Christ, so they live in “the dynamic realm or sphere” whose boundaries are defined by the Spirit (Heil 2007b: 507, 516).

If this is correct, however, Paul has still left the agent and the content of the filling undefined. Who fills believers, and with what are they to be filled? In 3:19 Paul prays that his readers might “be filled up to all the fullness of God” and in 4:13 he describes the growth of the church until it becomes “a mature man” and reaches “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ.” God seems to be the source of the filling in 3:19, just as he is probably the source of Christ’s fullness in 1:23, and the content of the fullness in 3:19 is probably the maturity that God wants the church to attain as it grows up to his fullness, or as 4:13 puts it, to the “fullness” of Christ’s stature. Here in 5:18, Paul says similarly that his readers should cooperate with the growth that God supplies toward the maturity he created them to attain (cf. 2:10, 15).

[5:19] Paul next says that as a result of their growth toward maturity in the realm of the Spirit (5:18; cf. 3:19; 4:13), his readers will meet together for praise of God and instruction. Paul expresses this in a series of participial constructions. The first of these, λαλοῦντες ἑαυτοῖς (lalountes heautois, speaking among yourselves), is dependent on the phrase πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι (plērousthe en pneumati, be filled in the Spirit) in 5:18. One result of being filled in the Spirit is speaking to one another in the form of ψαλμοί (psalmoi, psalms), ὕμνοι (hymnoi, hymns), and ᾠδὰ πνευματικαί (ōda pneumatikai, spiritual songs).[7] Paul may have intended to contrast the crude singing typical of Greco-Roman feasting (e.g., Propertius, Elegies 4.6.85–86; Quintilian, Inst. 1.2.8; cf. D’Ambra 2007: 55) with the Spirit-inspired singing of corporate Christian worship (e.g., Eadie 1883: 399; Swete 1909: 241).

These three terms were used by Greek-speaking Jewish authors of roughly Paul’s time to refer to songs of praise to God, including the songs in the canonical book of Psalms. In a fairly clear reference to the psalms of David, 2 Sam. 23:1 LXX says, “The psalms [ψαλμοί] of Israel are beautiful” (my trans.). Josephus tells us that David “composed songs [ᾠδάς] and hymns [ὕμνους] to God in varied meters” (Ant. 7.305, trans. Thackeray and Marcus 1926–81) and that when Judas Maccabaeus celebrated the rededication of the temple, he delighted the people and honored God “with hymns [ὕμνοις] and psalms [ψαλμοῖς]” (Ant. 12.323, my trans.).[8] Luke regularly uses the term ψαλμός for the material in the canonical book of Psalms (Luke 20:42; 24:44; Acts 1:20; 13:33), although Paul uses the same term to refer to a Spirit-inspired song that someone utters in a Christian assembly (1 Cor. 14:26; cf. 1 Cor. 14:15; James 5:13). Since the three terms seem almost interchangeable, and since Ephesians has a tendency to be redundant, it is probably a mistake to distinguish the terms sharply from one another (so correctly Gnilka 1971: 270; Lincoln 1990: 345; Schnackenburg 1991: 237). The adjective “spiritual,” however, which is attached to the last term, “songs,” probably does have special reference to the kind of spontaneous, Spirit-inspired singing to which 1 Cor. 14:15, 26 refer (Fee 1994: 653).[9]

All three kinds of singing are forms of “speaking” to one another within the worshiping community. Hymns in antiquity were sometimes in prose rather than poetic form and involved instruction as well as praise (Gordley 2007: 30–39), so the term “speaking” covers more than the singing of poetic compositions or utterances of praise to God. It also includes the kind of instruction that Paul assumes his readers have received, according to 4:20–21 (cf. Col. 3:16).

This musical speech is to be heartfelt and directed to the Lord. The two participles ᾄδοντες (adontes, singing) and ψάλλοντες (psallontes, making melody) are the verbal forms of the nouns ᾠδή (ōdē, song) and ψαλμός (psalmos, psalm). They stand parallel to λαλοῦντες and, like it, are subordinate to the main verb πληροῦσθε in 5:18 (Schnackenburg 1991: 238). They do not describe a separate action from “speaking” but give more detail about what this “speaking” involves. It involves singing and making melody “with the heart.” This is the inner human being, where Christ dwells (3:17). It is the aspect of his readers’ existence that Paul prays the Spirit would strengthen so that they might comprehend the vastness of Christ’s love (3:16–19). This is also the faculty that Paul prays for God to enlighten, by means of his Spirit, so that they might understand the vastness of the blessings he has given them in Christ (1:17–23). It is “with the heart,” then, that songs of praise for Christ’s love and God’s blessing through Christ are directed “to the Lord,” that is, to Christ (cf. 5:20).

[5:20] The participle εὐχαριστοῦντες (eucharistountes, giving thanks), like the three participles in the previous verse, is also subordinate to πληροῦσθε in 5:18. Thanks could certainly be given to God through singing (3 Macc. 7:16), but Paul may intend to shift the thought slightly to encourage corporate prayer. The only other use of the verb εὐχαριστέω (eucharisteō) in the letter refers to his own thanksgiving to God in prayer for his readers (1:16), and normally when people give thanks in the NT, they do so to God in prayer for some gift that he has given to them, such as food.[10] Paul views giving thanks to God as an obligation of all human beings (Rom. 1:21; 2 Thess. 1:3; 2:13), and thus, not surprisingly, giving thanks to God was part of corporate Christian worship (1 Cor. 14:16–17). It was an especially prominent part of the repeated observance of the Lord’s Supper (1 Cor. 11:24), which, as early as the Didache (ca. AD 100), was called “the Eucharist” (ἡ εὐχαριστία, hē eucharistia; 9.1, 5; cf. Ign. Phld. 4; Smyrn. 8.1; Schnackenburg 1991: 238n27).

Paul frequently spoke in expansive terms of giving thanks to God, just as he does here: he can say that he “always” (πάντοτε) thanks God for the congregations to whom he writes (1 Thess. 1:2; 1 Cor. 1:4; Philem. 4; Col. 1:3; cf. 1 Thess. 2:13) and can urge his readers to be thankful “in everything” (ἐν παντί, en panti; 1 Thess. 5:18; cf. Col. 3:17). Here, then, he is probably thinking of thanksgiving prayers offered during corporate worship, and the reference to doing this “always for all things” (πάντοτε ὑπὲρ πάντων, pantote hyper pantōn) is a typically Pauline way of saying that thanksgiving should be a constant theme. Those who are filled in the realm of the Spirit should generously and frequently express their thanks to God when they gather with others for worship. Perhaps Paul has in mind the context of Christian worship when he tells his readers in 5:4 to replace “obscenity,” “nonsensical talk,” and “suggestive witticism” with “thanksgiving” (εὐχαριστία).

Thanksgiving is given “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” a phrase that recalls the use of “the name of the LORD” to bless people in the OT (Deut. 21:5; 2 Sam. 6:18; 1 Chron. 16:2; Ps. 129:8). Paul, then, has used language to describe Jesus that in the OT is reserved for Yahweh, a move that is typical of the Christology of his other letters (cf. 2 Thess. 3:6; 1 Cor. 1:10; 5:3–4; Phil. 2:9–10; Fee 2007: 67–68, 135, 362). Jesus Christ is not identical with Yahweh, however, since thanksgiving is given in his name to “God, who is also Father” (τῷ θεῷ καὶ πατρί, tō theō kai patri). As the rest of the letter makes clear, God is the one who created the universe and who is now restoring it to its original unity in Christ (Eph. 1:10; 2:15; 3:9; 4:6). He is also the one whose fatherhood extends through his beloved Son Jesus to his chosen people (1:3–5). Blessings such as these, expressed so fully in the letter’s opening benediction, were probably among the subjects that Paul had in mind when he spoke of those filled in the realm of the Spirit giving corporate thanks to God in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ (cf. Best 1998: 513).

Summary

In 5:15–20 Paul begins the transition to a body of positive, practical advice about how his readers should live within a culture dominated by evil. They cannot simply relax and hope for the best, but instead need to be alert to how they are living, perceptive about the condition of the world around them, and sensitive to the Lord’s will. They should have nothing to do with the drunken debauchery that characterizes the prevailing culture but should live in the realm of the Spirit and grow in their maturity in Christ. As a result, they will gather with other Christians for instructional singing and for thanksgiving to God—the Father who has so richly blessed them through their union with the Lord Jesus Christ.



Additional Notes

5:19. The phrase [ἐν] ψαλμοῖς καὶ ὕμνοις καὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς comes with two primary textual problems. First, the preposition ἐν stands before the phrase in the two early Alexandrian manuscripts 𝔓46 and B and the later Alexandrian manuscripts P, 6, 33, and 1739. The evidence for including the preposition, then, is primarily Alexandrian. It is omitted in a range of manuscripts from the Alexandrian (א, A, Ψ), Western (D, F, G), and Byzantine (most) traditions. The diversity of witnesses to the text without the preposition probably means that a copyist added it, although this must have happened at a very early date (cf. Hoehner 2002: 707).

Second, 𝔓46 and B, two manuscripts of the Old Latin, and Ambrosiaster omit the adjective πνευματικαῖς at the end of the phrase. A wide geographical spread of witnesses, however, includes it. For example, א, Ψ, 33, 1739 (Alexandrian); D, F, G (Western); and the majority of Byzantine manuscripts have πνευματικαῖς. The internal evidence is evenly balanced. On one hand, it is easy to see how the wording of Col. 3:16 might have led a scribe to include the adjective, but on the other hand it is equally easy to see how a scribe’s eye might have accidentally skipped over πνευματικαῖς since its final syllable (ΑΙΣ) is identical to the final syllable of the previous word (ᾠδαῖς; Metzger 1994: 540–41). The geographical diversity of the witnesses to the inclusion of the adjective should probably prevail, tipping the scale in favor of keeping πνευματικαῖς in the text. In addition, πνευματικαῖς fits the context since Paul is explaining what happens in corporate worship when believers are filled in the realm of the Spirit (5:18).

5:20. Many English translations render the phrase τῷ θεῷ καὶ πατρί with “to God the Father,” as if Paul had written τῷ θεῷ πατρί (cf. 6:23; Col. 3:17). By inserting καί into the phrase, however, Paul has placed special emphasis on God’s identity not only as God but also as Father, and the translation “to God, who is also Father” tries to capture this emphasis.

The “Granville-Sharp” rule does apply to the phrase, but the rule is irrelevant to this particular problem (pace Hoehner 2002: 715).[11] The issue is not whether “God” and “Father” refer to the same person, something that is not in dispute, but how the καί should be interpreted (cf. Best 1998: 514).





XI. Wise Conduct within the Household (5:15–6:9)

A. Introduction: Wisdom and the Life Filled in the Spirit (5:15–20)

B. Submission in the Believing Household (5:21–6:9)


B. Submission in the Believing Household (5:21–6:9)

To begin a new major section of the epistle at this point may seem odd, since from a strictly grammatical perspective 5:21 sits in the middle of a sentence that runs from 5:18 to 5:22. The first term in this new section is the participle ὑποτασσόμενοι (hypotassomenoi, submitting), and grammatically speaking, it is simply the last of four participial elements that modify the phrase πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι (plērousthe en pneumati, be filled in the Spirit) in 5:18b. The grammatical structure of 5:18b–21 might be diagrammed this way:

Be filled in the Spirit,

speaking among yourselves with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs,

singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord,

giving thanks always for all things in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ to God, who is also Father,

submitting [ὑποτασσόμενοι] to each other in the fear of Christ.



This final participial element, however, stands apart from the other three elements conceptually and begins a lengthy section of its own. The other three elements all cluster around the theme of corporate worship. As the plural reflexive pronoun ἑαυτοῖς (heautois, among yourselves; v. 19) shows, the setting envisioned in 5:18b–20 is of believers gathering together for instruction, singing, and grateful prayer. The admonition to submit to one another, however, takes the ethical instruction in the new direction of household conduct, and soon even the grammar will reveal that a new major section has begun: in 5:24 the verb ὑποτάσσω (hypotassō, submit) is repeated, but this time in the indicative mood as the main verb in a new sentence. The phrase “submitting to one another in the fear of Christ,” then, functions at the same time as a transition from the previous section on corporate worship to the new section on submission and as a heading over the new section, indicating its primary concern—submission to one another in the household.

The transitional nature of the participle is important since in the ancient context of Ephesians the idea of Christians assembling together for worship and the idea of the household were closely connected. From Christianity’s beginnings through the end of the second century, Christians met for corporate worship in houses, and it seems likely that those in charge of these households, as the hosts of the meetings within them, had a strong influence over what took place there (Balla 2003: 174; Osiek and MacDonald 2006). Because of this, the movement from a description of corporate worship among believers filled “in the Spirit” to the subject of conduct within the household was natural. Since Paul addresses wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters directly, he probably envisions members of each group gathered within a house for worship and listening to this letter as it is read aloud.

The proper ordering of the household was a common topic in the philosophical and exhortatory literature of the Greco-Roman world. It was an important element in Plato’s political philosophy, and his own discussion of the household shows that he was taking up a topic that was already part of philosophical tradition (Balch 1981: 25). Aristotle also discussed household management under the heading of how to govern the city-state. His views were adopted and published in the mid-first century BC by Arius Didymus, the court philosopher of Augustus, and they reappear in Stoic, Jewish, Neo-Pythagorean, and early Christian texts (Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 48–50; Balch 1981: 22–59; 1988: 25–47). Since the topic is so common in extant Greco-Roman literature, it is not surprising that the early Christian discussions of household management resemble those of the prevailing culture (Col. 3:18–4:1; 1 Pet. 2:13–3:7; cf. 1 Tim. 2:1–3:13; 6:1–2; Titus 1:5–9; 2:2–10; 3:1; Did. 4.9–11; Ign. Pol. 4–5; Pol. Phil. 4.2–6.3; Barn. 19.5, 7; 1 Clem. 1.3; 21.6–8).[1]

Among NT scholars, sections of early Christian literature that cover domestic conduct are often labeled “household code” material.[2] This body of ethical instruction has been the object of intense scholarly scrutiny since the early twentieth century, much of it focused on the ultimate sources of the early Christian household codes (Balch 1981: 1–10; 1988: 25–50; Wagener 1994: 15–65). Did they derive from the world of ancient political philosophy, where the family was considered to be an essential component of the city-state (e.g., Aristotle, Pol. 1.3 [1.1253b.1–14]; 1.12 [1.1259a.37–1259b.17]; e.g., Balch 1981)? Or from the concern of Stoic philosophers with one’s “duty towards the gods, towards parents, towards brothers, towards my country, towards strangers” (Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 2.17.31], trans. W. Oldfather 1925–28; e.g., Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 48–50)? Or from a hypothetical set of traditions connected with the missionary work of Hellenistic Jews (cf., e.g., Philo, Hypoth. 7.1–9; Josephus, Ag. Ap. 2.190–219; Crouch 1972: 84–119)? Or from Greek collections of wise sayings, some of them having to do with the home (e.g., Pseudo-Plutarch, Lib. ed. 7e; Berger 1984: 135–41)?

One of the most influential explanations of the NT household codes sees them as primarily apologetic in character, a thesis that was argued by Balch (1981; 1988) with respect to 1 Peter. On this theory, the codes are best understood within the context of ancient political philosophy, where relationships within the household were sometimes linked in various ways with the government of the city-state. Plato (Resp. 4.433a–d), for example, claimed that justice was essential to governing the state, that justice, by definition, involved each person performing his or her assigned task, and that the city-state worked best when this sense of justice was internalized. This internalization of one’s assigned place was particularly helpful when it occurred within “child, woman, slave, free, artisan, ruler, and ruled” (trans. Shorey 1930–35; cf. Balch 1981: 24). Plato’s ideas on the justice of a household arrangement—where parents rank above their children and masters above their slaves, and the connection of this household structure to the government of the city—was already traditional by Plato’s time, argues Balch (Plato, Leg. 627; Balch 1981: 24–25).

Aristotle (Pol. 1.3 [1.1253b.1–3]) also discussed “the management of the household” (οἰκονομία, oikonomia) as part of political philosophy, “for every state,” he said, “is composed of households [οἰκιῶν, oikiōn]” (trans. Rackham 1990). He organized the household in a way that is reminiscent of the household codes in Col. 3:18–4:1 and Eph. 5:22–6:9: “The investigation of everything should begin with its smallest parts, and the primary and smallest parts of the household are master and slave, husband and wife, father and children; we ought therefore to examine the proper constitution and character of each of these three relationships” (Aristotle, Pol. 1.3 [1.1253b.1–9], trans. Rackham 1990; Balch 1981: 33).

This link between the state and the household—with the household defined in terms of a man’s relationship to wife, children, and slaves—continued to be important in discussions of domestic ethics for centuries after Plato and Aristotle. It was well known to Arius Didymus, the friend and court philosopher of Caesar Augustus in the first century BC, and reappears in Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Ant. rom. 2.25.4–5; 2.26.1, 3–4), Philo (Joseph 38–39; Spec. Laws 2.225–27; 3.169–71; Decalogue 165–67), and Josephus (Ag. Ap. 2.199), among others (Balch 1981: 40–43, 52–55).

Balch claims that Philo, Josephus, and the author of 1 Peter all used the Aristotelian household pattern in the first century to refute claims that their religious convictions were socially and politically subversive. Against opponents who said that Judaism undermined Roman marriage customs, Philo and Josephus argued that the Mosaic law supported the subordination of wives to husbands (Balch 1981: 74–76). Against the slanders of unbelievers (1 Pet. 2:11–12; 3:15–16), the author of 1 Peter urges the wives and slaves among his readers to fulfill societal expectations that they should be subordinate to their husbands and masters (2:13–3:7; Balch 1981: 81–116).

This understanding of the origin and late first-century use of the household codes has also influenced the interpretation of Ephesians. M. Y. MacDonald (2000), for example, acknowledges that there is no explicit indication of an apologetic purpose for the household code in Eph. 5:21–6:9. Nevertheless, she believes that Ephesians was written in a time and place where Christians were thought to be a social threat, and that the household code was part of a strategy to deal with this threat. It articulates a vision of the Christian home that outwardly looks no different from the highest societal expectations of the day but internally is radically different. Outwardly, Ephesians pictures the Christian paterfamilias as ruling benevolently over wife, children, and slaves according to prevailing cultural expectations, but inwardly the submission of the wife to the husband becomes a metaphor for the submission of the church to Christ. By identifying the wife with the church body, of which Christ is the head, moreover, the author of Ephesians detaches both the Christian home, and the church that meets there, from society and gives it a glorious place alongside the ascended Christ (5:23; cf. 1:19–23; 2:6). This strategy makes the church less visible within its hostile environment at the same time that it retains for the church a sense of separation from pagan society, with its futile way of life and darkened understanding (4:17–5:20; MacDonald 2000: 159–69; 337–38; Osiek and MacDonald 2006: 118–43; cf. Merz 2000: 132, 146).

There is certainly historical precedent for this way of understanding the household code in Ephesians. Hellenized Jews, such as Josephus and Philo, used the prevailing Greco-Roman household ideology to ease tensions between Jews and the societies in which they had to live (Josephus, Ag. Ap. 2.199–214; Philo, Decalogue 165–67; Barclay 2007: lii). Pseudo-Phocylides (175–227) probably used a “household code” in a similar but less defensive way to show Jewish readers that their traditional customs were compatible with the best ethical teaching of the Hellenistic world (W. Wilson 2005: 3–8). A good case can be made for viewing the household material in 1 Peter as part of an apologetic strategy for marginalized Christians.

The household code in Ephesians, however, is probably not part of a strategy to ease tensions between the church and society. Unlike 1 Peter (2:15; 3:1), Ephesians makes no attempt to link domestic ethics to either defending or promoting the faith among unbelievers (cf. Darko 2008: 99–100). How, then, does the household code function in Ephesians?

First, it continues the practical ethical instruction that has been the theme since 4:17. Paul needed no special reasons for including instruction on the household within this material. Household instruction following the three-pair pattern of husband-wife, parents-children, master-slave was commonly known for centuries on either side of the New Testament (Balch 1981: 21–62; 1988: 27). It was considered to be a normal topic for paraenetic or preceptorial advice in the first century (Seneca, Ep. 94.1), and it was natural—even expected—that Paul should include it in the letter at this point (cf. Col. 3:18–4:1).

Second, Paul wanted to use the first topic of the household code, marriage, to illustrate the close relationship between Christ and the church, a major theme in the first part of the letter. The ideas that Christ is the head of the church, that the church is Christ’s body, and that Christ works sacrificially for the benefit of the church—all these were important in 1:3–4:16. Paul now weaves these themes back into his moral instruction, and carries them further, by means of the household code (Osiek and MacDonald 2006: 126–31).

Scholars have often seen the use of the household code in Ephesians as a problem for the view that Ephesians is a genuine letter from Paul. Some believe that the code represents a post-Pauline stage in the effort to tame an early-Christian, Spirit-prompted emphasis on complete social equality within the church, an impulse visible in such texts as Gal. 3:28 (e.g., Crouch 1972: 120–45). Many see it as part of a more general trend in postapostolic Christianity to accommodate Christian ethics to prevailing societal structures (e.g., Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 48; Lincoln 1990: 360, 398; MacDonald 2000: 338).

Best believes that it betrays a level of idealism inconsistent with the genuine Paul’s pastoral sensitivity to conditions in the real world. The household code in Ephesians, he argues, pictures its readers living in entirely Christian households, whereas the authentic Paul understood the complex pastoral problems that come with the often-mixed households in which believers lived (Best 1997a: 193–94).

In the end, however, none of these arguments is compelling. It is difficult to see much development between the tone of the advice in 1 Thess. 4:11, “to aspire to live quietly and be busy with your own affairs and to work with your own hands,” and the tone of the household code here. The Paul of the undisputed letters, moreover, is as happy as the author of Ephesians to provide an ideal picture of those in authority in the course of an argument that his readers should submit to them (Rom. 13:1–7).

In Ephesians, then, the household code continues the kind of basic moral instruction that Paul believes is necessary for a wide audience of Gentile believers, at least some of whom badly need moral instruction. Prior to hearing and believing the gospel, they lived by “the cravings of” their “flesh” (2:3), were “without God in the world” (2:12), and blindly groped their way through a debauched existence (4:17–19). In the household code, he fashions advice on how those who have left that path should live now that they have been radically changed by the gospel. The framework for this advice arises from the first-century Greco-Roman environment in which Paul and his readers live, but he infuses that framework with the theology of the letter’s first three chapters.





1. Wives and Husbands (5:21–33)

Paul organizes his household instruction under three headings: wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters (cf. Col. 3:18–4:1). Unlike much household instruction from antiquity, Paul addresses the subordinate member of each pair directly. The subordinate members of each pair are not people who need to be managed for the benefit of the male household head, but members of the people of God, gifted for service (cf. 4:11–16) and in need of instruction on how to live in a way that is pleasing to God within the societal categories they occupy. Paul probably imagines both wives and husbands gathered with other believers within a house for worship and listening to his instruction as it is read aloud (cf. 5:19–20).

Paul’s instructions to wives and husbands is much longer than his advice to the other two pairs. The reason for this is probably twofold.

First, sexual ethics have figured prominently in the admonitions given so far and have taken a negative tone (4:19, 22, 29; 5:3–14). Here Paul provides a positive counterpart to those warnings against sexual perversion. The answer to sexual debauchery is not asceticism (cf. 1 Tim. 4:3) but keeping sexual relations within marriage, as God intended from the beginning when he created human beings in two genders.[1]

Second, unlike the other two pairs of relationships, the relationship between wife and husband portrays the relationship between the church and Christ. This theme of Christ’s benevolent authority over the church was richly developed in the first part of the letter by using the extended metaphor of a body and its head. In 1:22–23 Paul has said that Christ is the head over all things for the benefit of the church, which is his body. Then in 4:7–16 Christ becomes the head especially of his church body. In this role Christ supplies all that the body needs in order to grow to maturity and function smoothly. Now we learn that God has instituted marriage at creation “on account of” this relationship between the church and Christ (5:31). When the wife submits to the husband as her head (5:21–24), and when the husband loves, gives his life for, cherishes, and cares for his wife (5:25–29a), then their union with each other depicts the union between Christ and the church (5:29b–31). That human marriage has this significance, Paul concludes, is a “great mystery” (5:32)—something that would have been unknown if God had not revealed it. It is probably because of the unusual significance of this particular relationship that Paul treats it first among the household pairs, and at greatest length.

Paul weaves this complex theology with straightforward ethical instruction throughout the section. His instruction to wives begins (5:21–22) and ends (5:24b) with practical encouragement to submit to their husbands, but sandwiched between these two admonitions is the comparison between Christ’s saving authority over the church and the husband’s authority over the wife (5:22–23a). Similarly, his instruction to husbands begins (5:25a) and ends (5:33a–b) with the practical admonition to them to love their wives and is punctuated in the middle (5:28–29a) with a relatively lengthy description of what this means in practical terms. Again, however, the comparison between Christ’s self-giving love for the church and the husband’s love for his wife appears between these layers of practical advice.

Paul’s main concern throughout the section, both in practical and theological terms, is with the husband’s love for his wife and Christ’s love for the church. This is clear not only from the relative length of the material devoted to wives and husbands, but also from the summary of Paul’s practical advice to both in 5:33. Both the rhetorical forcefulness and the number of words in that concluding statement devoted to the husband’s love for his wife (5:33a–b) outweigh the delicately phrased and brief admonition to the wife to fear her husband (5:33c). Paul places the burden of this section on the husband, whose headship must be expressed not in managing his wife but in meeting her physical and emotional needs (5:29), in short, in giving his own life for hers (5:25).



Exegesis and Exposition

21Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ, 22wives ⌜ ⌝ to your own husbands as to the Lord 23because the husband is the head of the wife in the same way that Christ is head of the church—he himself is Savior of the body. 24But as the church submits to Christ, so also wives to husbands in everything.

25Husbands, love your wives just as Christ loved the church and gave himself for her 26that he might sanctify her by means of cleansing [her] with the water bath in the word 27⌜that he might present⌝ the church to himself as brilliant, not having spot or wrinkle or any such things, but that she might be holy and blameless. 28So husbands are obligated to love their own wives as their own bodies. The one who loves his own wife loves himself. 29For no one ever hated his own flesh, but he cares for and cherishes it just as Christ also did for the church 30because we are parts of his body ⌜ ⌝. 31On account of this, a man will leave his father and his mother and will cling to his wife, and the two will be one flesh. 32This mystery is great, but I am talking about Christ and the church. 33In any case, you too—every single one of you—must love his own wife in this way: as himself. And the wife should fear her husband.

[5:21] Some commentators (e.g., Best 1998: 515–16) attach this verse to the previous section, and the grammatical structure of the passage certainly supports this view. Ὑποτασσόμενοι (hypotassomenoi, submitting) is one of a string of five participles in 5:19–21 that qualify πληροῦσθε (plērousthe, be filled), and so at one level it makes sense to see “submitting to one another” as a description of yet another result of being filled in the sphere of the Spirit: those who are filled in the Spirit not only speak, sing, make melody, and give thanks in corporate worship; they also submit to one another in the fear of Christ.

The theme of submission, however, dominates the household code that follows, reappearing not only where the term ὑποτάσσω (hypotassō, submit) itself is implied (5:22) or used (5:24), but also where the concepts of fear (5:33; 6:5), honor (6:2), and obedience (6:1, 5) show up. The grammatical attachment of the participle to the previous section eases the transition to the new section, but the substance of the verse, with its focus on submission, means that it is best taken with what follows and should be understood as an introduction to it (cf. Dawes 1998: 18–21).

This transitional “messiness” is perhaps another signal of the oral nature of this text. Paul was composing his text as he dictated it, although with a traditional outline of household duties in mind.

The verb ὑποτάσσω refers to the ordering of something underneath something else, and when the passive voice of the verb is used of people (as it is here), it often refers to the voluntary “submission” of one person to another (BDAG 1042). People should place their minds underneath God’s authority (but often do not do this; Rom. 8:7; cf. 10:3); people should place themselves under the divinely ordained governmental authorities (Rom. 13:1, 5; Titus 3:1); the Corinthian church should submit to the household of Stephanas (1 Cor. 16:16); wives should, similarly, submit themselves to their husbands (Col. 3:18; Titus 2:5), and slaves should do the same with respect to their masters (Titus 2:9).

How is it possible to submit in this way “to one another” (ἀλλήλοις, allēlois)? Certainly it seems impossible for God or governmental authorities to submit to their subjects just as their subjects submit to them, and Paul proceeds in the household code that follows 5:21 to speak of the submission and obedience only of wives, children, and slaves, not of husbands, parents, and masters. Interpreters have tried to explain this problem in basically three ways.

First, some have thought that “submitting to one another” refers to mutual submission and states the author’s real view, but that the traditional pattern of subordination in the household code contradicts this view. The author allows an inconsistently authoritarian ethic from the tradition that he uses to slip through his editorial net, but the mutuality expressed in 5:21 “reveals where the writer’s real interest lies” (Muddiman 2001: 254, 257; cf. Schnackenburg 1991: 245).

Second, some have thought that in 5:21 the topic of submission is announced and that in 5:22–6:9 Paul gives illustrations of how this submission “to one another” should work. The pronoun ἀλλήλοις does not mean that all believers are to submit to all other believers but that, among believers, submission should take place as it is described in 5:22–6:9. Theodoret had already taken this position in the fifth century (R. Hill 2001: 2.52), and it has been taken by many others since then (e.g., Ellicott 1859: 126; Robinson 1904: 123; O’Brien 1999: 401–4; Hoehner 2002: 717; Walden 2003: 254).

Third, some have understood Paul to be saying that there is a sense in which even those in authority “submit” to their subordinates. If Paul, who considered himself to be an authoritative apostle, could speak of becoming a slave (δουλόω, douloō) to all (1 Cor. 9:19), and could command all the Galatian Christians to “serve as each other’s slave [δουλεύετε ἀλλήλοις, douleuete allēlois] through love” (Gal. 5:13), then he could also speak both of “submitting to one another” and of exercising authority without contradiction (Jerome [Heine 2002]: 231). “Even kings and governors,” says Calvin (1965: 204), “rule that they may serve.” In the household code that follows 5:21, then, there is a sense in which husbands, fathers, and masters submit to those over whom they have authority, although the terms ὑποτάσσω or ὑπακούω (hypakouō) are not used of their responsibilities. Although the head of the household retains his position of authority, his use of that authority is tempered by an attitude of service to those over whom he has been placed (cf. Eadie 1883: 407; Bruce 1984: 382; Lincoln 1990: 366; Best 1998: 516–17; Helton 2005: 33–41).

The first explanation has little to be said for it. The author’s own approach to the traditional household code is deeply etched into his version of it (5:25–30; 6:4, 9), and this makes it unlikely that he would have carelessly allowed a contradictory note of authoritarianism to remain unchanged.

The second explanation is much more likely, and it has the great merit of assigning to the term ὑποτάσσω its normal meaning of “accepting the exact place God has assigned, keeping to one’s rank in this or that society, accepting a dependent status” (Spicq, TLNT 3:425). Advocates of this approach are correct to say that the mere occurrence of the reciprocal pronoun in the phrase “submitting to one another” poses no difficulty for their position: the term ἀλλήλων does not need to refer to an action that everyone does to everyone else (e.g., Gal. 6:2; Rev. 6:4; O’Brien 1999: 403).

Still, the third explanation is best. Paul’s use of the notion of reciprocity so far in Ephesians leads the letter’s readers to understand the pronoun here in a fully reciprocal sense. The letter has just spoken of bearing with “each other” (4:2), being members of “one another” (4:25), and being kind to “one another” (4:32), using ἀλλήλων in each case to refer to expectations of all believers. To hear now of “submitting to one another” might seem slightly strange, but it does hint that there is a sense in which everyone is involved in serving others.

That this idea would not be unintelligible is clear from 1 Cor. 16:15–16.[2] There Paul says that the members of Stephanas’s household in Corinth “placed themselves at the service of the saints” (εἰς διακονίαν τοῖς ἁγίοις ἔταξαν ἑαυτούς, eis diakonian tois hagiois etaxan heautous). He then urges the Corinthian believers generally to “submit [ὑποτάσσησθε, hypotassēsthe] to such people.” There may be a difference between placing oneself in the service (εἰς διακονίαν . . . τάσσω, eis diakonian . . . tassō) of others and submitting to others (ὑποτάσσω), but it is not large.

The submission of those mentioned in the household code is not the same type in each instance—in the code itself, husbands, fathers, and masters are never told to submit to, obey, or fear their wives, children, and slaves—but the instructions to the head of the household do rein in his power, and the entire code closes with a sober warning that he too is under the authority of God, who is no respecter of persons (Eph. 6:9). The mutuality of the code and the restraint that it places on the one in authority make it likely that the odd expression “submit to one another” means more than simply “obey whom you are supposed to” (trans. Walden 2003: 254). It certainly includes this meaning, but it also prepares the ground for the distinctive approach that the household code takes to the responsibilities of husbands, fathers, and masters.

The concluding phrase urges the letter’s readers to submit to one another in the φόβος (phobos) that Christ’s position of authority demands.[3] Φόβος can be used negatively to mean “intimidation” (e.g., 1 Pet. 3:14), something that produces fear (e.g., Rom. 13:3), or “fear” itself (e.g., 2 Cor. 7:5).[4] It can also have the positive connotation of showing respect to someone who, because of their position of authority or power, deserves obedience or deference (e.g., Rom. 13:7; Eph. 6:5; 1 Pet. 2:18; 3:2, 15). In both the LXX and NT, φόβος is considered an appropriate attitude to have toward God (e.g., Pss. 33:12 LXX [34:11 MT, Eng.]; 35:2 LXX [36:2 MT; 36:1 Eng.]; 2 Cor. 7:1; Rom. 3:18).[5] In 2 Cor. 5:10–11 the fear of Christ is linked to the day when “all of us will appear before the judgment seat of Christ,” but in Rom. 8:15 Paul says that because God is the father of believers, they do not need to fear him as a slave would fear a master (cf. 1 John 4:18).

The fear of Christ that motivates believers to submit to one another, then, is something more than deference but less than terror (Hoehner 2002: 719). It seems to be a respect for Christ, to whom God has subjected (ὑπέταξεν, hypetaxen) all the inimical powers of the universe (1:22; 4:8–10), and as a consequence of his position, a fear of disobeying him. Since Christ’s self-sacrificing grace and love (1:7; 5:2, 25) are integral to his position of authority, however, this appropriate fear must be tempered with a knowledge of the incomprehensible vastness of his love (3:18–19).

[5:22] Paul begins his version of the household code, just as he does in Colossians (3:18), with instructions to wives, and this initiates a pattern he will follow throughout the code. Paul does not simply issue instructions to the male head of the household about how he should govern his estate (as in Ps.-Phoc. 195–227), nor does he discuss “household management” as an abstract philosophical topic (as in Aristotle, Pol. 1.1–13 [1.1252a.1–1260b.24]; Josephus, Ag. Ap. 199–206); instead he gives instructions to each member of the three traditional pairs, and in each case he begins with the subordinate member of the pair. Wives are addressed as equal to husbands in the responsibility they bear for their behavior. This approach is certainly not unprecedented in Greco-Roman moral discourse (cf. Pseudo-Aristotle, Oec. 3.140–47), but Paul’s understanding of the equality of men and women owes more to the OT than to these discussions (cf. 5:31; 6:2; Gen. 2:24; Exod. 20:12; Deut. 5:16)

The responsibility that Paul emphasizes here is the submissiveness of wives to their husbands. Some form of the verb ὑποτασσόμενοι (hypotassomenoi) in 5:21 must be mentally supplied to make sense of the statement (cf. 5:24). The lack of an explicit verb, however, is not unimportant. It tightens the connection between 5:21 and 5:22 and shows that Paul is describing here in 5:22 how wives can live out the instructions on submission that in 5:21 he gave to everyone. Believers should submit to one another, he says, and wives, for their part, should submit to their husbands.

Paul qualifies this admonition in two ways. First, wives are to submit to their “own” (ἴδιος, idios) husbands.[6] Later Paul will say that husbands should love “their own” (ἑαυτῶν, heautōn) wives (v. 28; cf. v. 33). This has the effect of restricting his comments on men and women in 5:22–24 to the marriage relationship (cf. Pol. Phil. 4.2). In contrast to Aristotle and the widely influential tradition he spawned, there is nothing here about the natural inferiority of women to men and the appropriateness, then, of men ruling over women.[7] There is certainly no hint that all women should submit to all men (so correctly Hoehner 2002: 732; Muddiman 2001: 258).[8]

Second, wives are to submit to their husbands “as to the Lord” (ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ, hōs tō kyriō). This phrase is ambiguous. A few earlier interpreters thought that the term κύριος here meant “master” and that Paul was telling wives to view their husbands as their masters.[9] That would have required the plural rather than the singular, however, and is not consistent with 6:5, 7, where Paul tells slaves to render obedience to their masters “as to Christ” and “as for the Lord and not for human beings.”

It is more difficult to decide the force of the ὡς. Does it mean that wives should submit to their husbands as if their husbands were Christ? This understanding seems consistent with the statements that follow in 5:23–24, where the husband’s role as head of the wife is compared to (ὡς) Christ’s role as head of the church. Or does it mean that when wives submit to their husbands, they are submitting to Christ because they are doing what Christ wants them to do? This seems consistent both with 6:7, where Paul urges slaves to work with goodwill since they are working for the Lord and not for human beings, and with Col. 3:18, where wives are urged to submit to their husbands “as is fitting in the Lord” (ὡς ἀνῆκεν ἐν κυρίῳ, hōs anēken en kyriō).

A decision between these two approaches is difficult, but the phrase “as to the Lord” here should probably be interpreted in light of the closely similar but clearer phrase “as for the Lord and not for human beings” in 6:7. Throughout the household code (5:22; 6:1, 5, 7), those who are asked to submit or to obey are asked to view their submission to others as part of their commitment to the Lord. The person to whom they submit does not have the authority of Christ, except in the case of marriage, and then only by analogy, not in reality. Christ is the submissive party’s authority, and when wives, children, and slaves render obedience, they do so out of obedience to Christ, not because of any innate authority in the male head of the household.

[5:23] Why should a wife’s commitment to the Lord lead her to submit to her husband? The ὅτι (hoti, because) clause answers this question by setting up an analogy between a married couple and Christ’s relationship to the church.

The term “head” (κεφαλή, kephalē) is the critical element in the analogy, but its precise meaning is not self-evident.[10] It was not commonly used in ancient Greek as a metaphor for an authority or leader (Perriman 1994: 602–10), although it does appear in the LXX with these connotations (Judg. 11:11; 2 Sam. 22:44; pace Perriman 1994: 603, 605). In each case, however, the person designated as the “head” has authority over groups of people, not over a single person, as is the case here (Perriman 1994: 619; Osiek 2002: 35).[11] A few interpreters, aware of the ambiguity of the term, have argued that there are no connotations of authority in Paul’s use of it in 5:23. Κεφαλή implies that the husband is the resource for the fulfillment of the wife, just as in 4:15–16 Christ, as the head of his church-body, equips and encourages the church’s growth (e.g., B. Mickelsen and A. Mickelsen 1986: 108–10).

This understanding of the term, however, is unlikely to be correct for two reasons. First, the context makes it clear that κεφαλή here carries overtones of authority. The instruction to the wife to “fear” her husband in 5:33 (cf. v. 21), advice not repeated to the husband, reveals a hierarchical element in the advice to wives and husbands generally and makes it likely that both Paul and his readers would have understood κεφαλή to have overtones of authority. This conclusion becomes virtually unavoidable when we look at the close verbal relationship between 5:21–23 and 1:20–23. In 1:20–23 Christ’s position as head (κεφαλή) over all things is defined in terms of God’s subjection (ὑποτάσσω, hypotassō) of all things to Christ. This same pairing of the noun κεφαλή with the verb ὑποτάσσω in 5:21–23 indicates that here too κεφαλή carries an authoritative nuance.[12]

Second, the cultural expectations of Paul’s readers led them to understand κεφαλή as a metaphor for the husband’s authority in the marriage relationship. Plutarch’s approach to marriage in the late first century was not everyone’s view,[13] but it still expresses the ideal many people in the Eastern Empire envisioned:

If [women] subordinate [ὑποτάττουσαι, hypotattousai] themselves to their husbands, they are commended, but if they want to have control, they cut a sorrier figure than the subjects of their control. And control ought to be exercised [κρατεῖν, kratein] by the man over the woman, not as the owner has control of a piece of property, but, as the soul controls the body [σώματος, sōmatos], by entering into her feelings and being knit to her through good will. As, therefore, it is possible to exercise care over the body [σώματος] without being a slave to its pleasure and desires, so it is possible to govern [ἄρχειν, archein] a wife, and at the same time to delight and gratify her. (Conj. praec. 142e; cf. 139a, d)[14]

This passage reveals that when Greco-Roman moral discourse on marriage uses “submission” language and “body” language in the same context, the body language typically illustrates the wife’s submission to the husband and the husband’s authority over the wife (Merz 2000: 132–33n4).

The differences between Plutarch and Paul, however, are also important. Plutarch’s advice is motivated by practical considerations (Conj. praec. 138b)—but Paul’s advice arises from his Christology (vv. 23b–24). Plutarch advises the husband to exercise power or “control” (κρατεῖν, kratein) over the wife, however benevolently, but Paul never tells husbands to control their wives, only wives to submit to their husbands. Despite some tender moments of mutuality in Plutarch’s essay, moreover, there is nothing to compare with the implications of what Paul does next.[15]

He immediately qualifies the husband’s authority by describing his headship as patterned after Christ’s headship over the church.[16] In Ephesians, Christ’s authority has been used not to control the church but to reconcile it to God at the cost of his own life (2:13, 16; 5:2; cf. 1:7) and to equip the church with what it needs for accomplishing God’s purposes (4:7–16).

As if to be sure that no one among his readers should miss this unusual element in Christ’s exercise of his position of authority, Paul restates it in terms that are both emphatic and explicit: “He himself [αὐτός, autos] is Savior of the body [σώματος, sōmatos].” Grammatically and rhetorically, this comment precisely matches the statement that Christ is head of the church, and this parallelism in the two phrases shows where Paul’s primary concern lies in using the term “head” to refer to Christ. Although κεφαλή implies authority, Paul correlates the term with σωτήρ (sōtēr). By doing this, he affirms Christ’s authority over the church, but his primary emphasis lies in his use of this authority to save the church:

Subject Predicate Genitive qualifier

ὁ Χριστός (ho Christos, Christ) κεφαλή (kephalē, head) τῆς ἐκκλησίας (tēs ekklēsias, of the church)

αὐτός (autos, he himself) σωτήρ (sōtēr, savior) τοῦ σώματος (tou sōmatos, of the body)

This correlation between Christ’s role as head and his role as Savior is reminiscent of passages in the first part of the letter in which Christ has used his authority and power for the church’s benefit. In 1:22–23 Paul has said that God has placed Christ in authority over all things, including the evil spiritual powers, for the benefit of the church, “which is his body [σῶμα, sōma],” and more recently he has said that the victorious Christ is the head of the body and directs its growth from this position of authority (4:15–16).[17]

Paul pictures the wife’s submission as the recognition of the authority of a husband who imitates the self-sacrificial, nurturing, and supporting roles that Christ fills with respect to the church. He will explore this theme in greater detail when he turns to the husband in 5:25–33, but this brief statement about the saving role of Christ with respect to the church anticipates that theme and shows how important it is to the whole account of the relationship between wife and husband.

[5:24] Paul seems to have caught himself drifting away from the practical to the theoretical in the final clause of 5:23: “He himself is the Savior of the body.” With ἀλλά (alla, but) he pulls his train of thought quickly back on track just as he will at the end of the passage in 5:33: “In any case, you too—every single one of you—must love his own wife.”[18] Both phrases are evidence that Ephesians started life as an oral discourse that, although not unorganized, was also not planned in meticulous detail.

Paul returns, then, to the practical concern of 5:22–23a and summarizes the primary intention of that statement. He again uses the verb ὑποτάσσω in the first clause and expects the reader (or hearer) to supply it in the second clause, and he again draws a comparison between the church’s subordinate position with respect to Christ and the subordinate position of wives with respect to their husbands.

Here, however, he adds that wives should submit to their husbands “in everything” (ἐν παντί, en panti). The sweeping nature of this phrase has prompted vigorous discussion among interpreters, and the discussion can be divided into two broad categories.

Some interpreters believe that the author simply made a mistake. Best (1998), in a way that is consistent with his approach to the household code generally, thinks the author had an unrealistic notion of marriage, imagining that husbands would micromanage their households and wives would submit to their management in every detail. Unlike the more-realistic Paul of the undisputed letters, the author imagines that every household where his letter is read is a Christian household and that every Christian husband will manage his household appropriately (Best 1998: 538). Muddiman (2001: 263), more charitably, thinks that the author simply allowed his enthusiasm for the church’s all-encompassing submission to Christ to “spill over” into his instructions about the wife’s submission to the husband. In one case such submission is appropriate, but in the other it is inappropriate (cf. Aletti 2001: 278).

Other interpreters think that Paul, or the author, would assume that the phrase needs to be qualified. His emphasis lies on complete obedience to the husband, but he would assume either that the comparison of the husband with Christ would qualify the sweeping nature of the phrase (Lincoln 1990: 373; Pokorný 1992: 222; Yoder Neufeld 2002: 256), or that his readers’ common sense would prevent them from thinking, for example, that wives should obey husbands who tell them to disobey God (Eadie 1883: 413; O’Brien 1999: 418; Hoehner 2002: 745–46).

This second approach must be correct. The phrase ἐν παντί, particularly in a text as effusive in its language as Ephesians, is not intended to be taken woodenly to mean “in everything no matter how harmful, silly, or sinful.” When Paul tells the Corinthians that he was “oppressed in every way [ἐν παντί]” in 2 Cor. 4:8 and 7:5, he does not mean that he bore every known affliction but that he faced much trouble (cf. 2 Cor. 9:8, 11; 11:6). So here he would assume that his readers understood the expansive nature of his language, appreciate the general point, and make exceptions in the hard cases where necessary.

That this interpretation is on the right track is also clear from the assumptions that lie beneath the discussion of a nearly identical problem in Paul’s Stoic contemporary Musonius Rufus.[19] When a young man who had been forbidden from studying philosophy by his father asked Musonius whether one must “obey one’s parents in all things [πάντα, panta],” the philosopher produced a series of examples in which a father instructs his child to do something harmful out of ignorance or to do something wrong out of wickedness. At the end of his list, he comments that “even to ask the question” of whether compliance is required in such cases “is scarcely necessary” (οὐδὲ ἐρωτᾶν τοῦτό γε ἄξιον, oude erōtan touto ge axion). He then goes on to apply the principle behind these obvious cases to the study of philosophy, where its application was less obvious.

This account is instructive because it shows both that the sweeping principle of obedience to parents “in everything” was commonly accepted in Paul’s time (cf. Col. 3:20) and that the principle was commonly understood not to apply in cases where ignorance, harm, or wrongdoing came into play. In the same way, Paul probably would have thought that when difficult situations arose, wives should use their discernment in “find[ing] out what is pleasing to the Lord” (5:10) and in doing it, although that might mean noncompliance with their husband’s wishes.[20]

This is assumed, however, and is not where the emphasis lies. The rhetorical force of ἐν παντί is focused on the importance of the wife’s submission to the husband. When the situation is not complicated by ignorant or immoral behavior, the wife should voluntarily submit to the leadership of her husband.

[5:25] Paul now turns to the responsibility that husbands have toward their wives. Once again, the analogy between Christ and the church is critical to his instructions, and once again, Christ’s work on behalf of the church is the critical element in the analogy. In 5:23 Paul has said that Christ is the Savior of the church, and here he explains how he has become the church’s Savior: he “gave himself for her.” This has happened as a demonstration of his love, and this is the kind of love, Paul says, that husbands should have for their wives.[21] The sweeping nature of the demand placed on the wife (ἐν παντί, en panti, in everything; v. 23) is therefore matched by an equally sweeping demand on the husband. Like Christ, the husband is to love (ἀγαπάω, agapaō) his wife by the sacrifice of his own life on his wife’s behalf (cf. 1:7; 2:13–16; 5:2).[22]

Here Paul breaks the boundaries of traditional Greco-Roman advice on marriage. It is not as if there are no expressions of tenderness, complementarity, and love in the traditional handbooks. “Love [στέργε, sterge] your wife,” advises Pseudo-Phocylides (195–97, trans. W. Wilson 2005), “for what is sweeter and better than when a wife is lovingly disposed [φρονέῃ φίλα, phroneē phila] to her husband into old age and husband to his wife and strife does not split them asunder.” “The co-operation between woman and man aims not merely at existence,” says Pseudo-Aristotle (Oec. 1.3.3, Tredennick and Armstrong 1935), “but at a happy existence.” According to Musonius Rufus, “In marriage there must be above all perfect companionship and mutual love [κηδεμονία, kēdemonia] of husband and wife, both in health and in sickness and under all conditions” (Lutz 1947: 88 lines 17–20; cf. Best 1998: 539).[23] “The marriage of a couple in love with each other,” Plutarch says, “is an intimate union,” similar to the organic unity of a living creature (Conj. praec. 142f, trans. Babbitt 1927–36).[24]

The idea that the husband should expend his life in the care of his wife, however, is unusual. The far more typical approach to marriage was that the wife should manage the household well in order to free the husband from domestic concerns and enhance his social prestige.[25] In contrast, Paul’s comparison between the husband’s love for his wife and Christ’s love for the church implies that the husband’s love for his wife should be so broad and long and high and deep (3:18–19) that it includes the sacrifice of his own social prestige and well-being, indeed his life, for the sake of his wife (cf. Phil. 2:5–8).

[5:26] The analogy between the love of husbands for their wives and the love of Christ for the church leads to a digression on the relationship between Christ and the church similar to, but much longer than, the digression in 5:22: “He himself is the Savior of the body.”[26] This digression stretches from 5:26 to 5:27 and takes the form of two purpose clauses, the second of which is more elaborate and contains a purpose clause of its own (cf. 3:16–19).[27] The first clause states the purpose for which Christ gave himself for the church (that he might sanctify it), and the second clause states the purpose for which Christ sanctified the church (that he might present her to himself in splendor). The second clause is more elaborate than the first clause and clarifies that Paul thinks of the sanctification and splendor of the church in moral terms.

First, Paul states why Christ gave himself for the church. He did this to “sanctify” (ἁγιάζω, hagiazō) the church, or to set it apart. The verb ἁγιάζω shows up only here in Ephesians, but the noun form of the adjective ἅγιος (hagios, holy) is Paul’s preferred term of identity for himself and his readers. They are “saints” (1:1, 15, 18; 2:19; 3:8, 18; 4:12; 5:3; 6:18), the people whom God has freely chosen to set apart as his heirs (1:18).

This consecration of the church as the people of God was accomplished “by means of cleansing” (καθαρίσας, katharisas) the church.[28] The term καθαρίζω (katharizō) was used in antiquity in agricultural and architectural contexts to refer to sifting grain, pruning plants, or clearing a building site (LSJ 850; LSJSup 162; MM 311). In the LXX it frequently refers to ritual cleansing (e.g., 1 Sam. 20:26; Neh. 12:30 [2 Esd. 22:30]; Jdt. 16:18; 1 Macc. 4:36, 41, 43), and sometimes in this context it is coupled with the verb ἁγιάζω (hagiazō) just as it is here (Exod. 29:36–37; Lev. 8:15; 16:19; cf. Pss. Sol. 17:30). When the two actions are viewed as separate from each other, cleansing comes first and leads to sanctification: it is the purification of the altar, for example, that sanctifies it (Exod. 29:36–37; Lev. 8:15; 16:18–19; cf. 2 Cor. 7:1). In the LXX, the NT, and nonbiblical Greek, the term could refer metaphorically to cleansing from sin (e.g., Exod. 20:7; 34:7; Num. 14:18; Ps. 50:4 [51:4 MT; 51:2 Eng.]; 2 Cor. 7:1; James 4:8; Heb. 10:2; Titus 2:14; Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 2.16.45]), and that is undoubtedly how Paul intends it here.[29] When the church was cleansed from its sin, it was then set apart as the people of God.

How has this cleansing happened? Viewed from one angle, it happened when Christ gave himself for the church, since the purpose of this giving was to sanctify it, and its sanctification involved its cleansing. Paul adds a phrase to the term καθαρίσας, however, to view the cleansing from another angle. Paul says that the cleansing took place “with the water bath in the word” (τῷ λουτρῷ τοῦ ὕδατος ἐν ῥήματι, tō loutrō tou hydatos en rhēmati).[30]

Through the centuries the vast majority of interpreters have thought that this phrase refers to baptism. Many simply assume this without argument. Those who do offer reasons for this reading explain that the article preceding λουτρῷ (loutrō) points to a specific event (the bath) and that this event is most likely baptism (Lincoln 1990: 375; Best 1998: 543); that much the same language appears in 1 Cor. 6:11, where Paul probably also refers to baptism (Lincoln 1990: 375; cf. Best 1998: 542); that the mention of water refers to a literal water rite, not to a metaphorical washing (Lincoln 1990: 375; Schnackenburg 1991: 249); and that the text finds a parallel in 1 Cor. 12:13, where the unity of the church originates with the common baptism of its members, a theme that the author of Epheisans has already picked up in 4:2–5 and that he will articulate again in 5:30 (Pokorný 1992: 224n45).

None of these arguments, however, is particularly compelling. The article may point to a particular water bath, but if the reference is metaphorical, it need not refer to the literal water bath of Christian baptism. There were many occasions for ceremonial washing with water in antiquity, and it was a common custom across a number of cultures for the bride to wash in water or touch water either in preparation for the wedding or as part of the ceremony.[31] To refer to “the bath of water,” then, would not necessarily have recalled the specific water rite of baptism. The reference to washing and sanctifying in 1 Cor. 6:11, moreover, is as ambiguous as this reference.
