There too the washing could easily refer to a spiritual rather than a physical washing, just as the expressions that follow it (“You were sanctified, . . . you were justified”) refer to spiritual realities. The parallel with 1 Cor. 12:13 actually highlights the most difficult problem for those who think that Eph. 5:26 refers to baptism. In 1 Cor. 12:13 Paul uses the verb βαπτίζω (baptizō), the common word for “baptizing” people in the NT, and the word whose noun form (βάπτισμα, baptisma) Paul does not hesitate to use in Eph. 4:5. Here, however, the word is λουτρόν (loutron), the term commonly used for ceremonial baths in antiquity and frequently occurring in connection with bridal baths (LSJ 1061; Spicq, TLNT 2:413n19).[32] In light of all this, the minority of interpreters who argue that the phrase “with the water bath” is a metaphorical reference to the cleansing power of the gospel are probably correct (e.g., O’Brien 1999: 422–24; Hoehner 2002: 752–54).

The final phrase in the clause, ἐν ῥήματι (en rhēmati, by the word), is difficult. It could modify one or both of the verbal elements in the clause and express the means by which the sanctifying, the cleansing, or both actions together, take place.[33] Alternatively, it could modify the phrase τῷ λουτρῷ τοῦ ὕδατος (tō loutrō tou hydatos) and describe something that accompanies “the water bath.”[34] In addition to this ambiguity, the meaning of the term ῥῆμα (rhēma) here is not clear. In the singular it can refer to an utterance, to a verbally describable event, or in early Christianity, to the teaching of God or the gospel (BDAG 905). It could refer, therefore, to a liturgical phrase uttered at baptism, perhaps the names of the three persons of the Trinity (e.g., Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 11 [NPNF 13:105]; Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.52]) or the name of Jesus (Robinson 1904: 207), or it could refer to the gospel, which those who belong to the church have believed (e.g., Ellicott 1859: 130; O’Brien 1999: 423; Hoehner 2002: 575–76).

Although settled pronouncements on such an ambiguous expression would be unwise, it seems simplest to take the phrase ἐν ῥήματι with the phrase τῷ λουτρῷ τοῦ ὕδατος, which immediately precedes it (cf. 2:15; 4:19; 6:2). It is true that Paul could easily have placed an article in front of ἐν ῥήματι (whether τῷ or τοῦ) to make this attachment explicit (Alford 1857: 133; Hoehner 2002: 757). Yet he does not do this when he uses an ἐν phrase at the end of a clause in 2:15; 4:19; and 6:2 (cf. De Wette 1843: 151; Schlier 1957: 257), and he probably would have placed ἐν ῥήματι closer to the verbal elements if he had intended the phrase to modify one or more of them.[35]

It also seems simplest to take the term ῥῆμα as a reference not to a baptismal formula but to the word of God, and even more specifically to the gospel, whose preaching brings the church into existence as people hear and believe it (cf. 1:13–14). Elsewhere in the NT ῥῆμα never refers to something spoken at baptism (Hoehner 2002: 755); in its only other use in Ephesians (6:17), Paul defines it more closely as “the word of God” (ῥῆμα θεοῦ, rhēma theou), and the term appears elsewhere in the NT with reference to the gospel that Paul and others have preached (Rom. 10:8, 16–17; Heb. 6:5; 1 Pet. 1:25; BDAG 905).

How, then, should we understand the phrase ἐν ῥήματι? The use of the idiom λούω ἐν (louō en) to refer to washing in a particular substance may offer a clue (cf. the LXX of Exod. 29:4; Lev. 14:8; 1 Kings 20:19; 22:38; Ps. 6:7 LXX, MT [6:6 Eng.]; Song 5:12; Ezek. 16:9).[36] If the phrase τῷ λουτρῷ τοῦ ὕδατος is taken as a unit to refer metaphorically to “the water bath,” then ἐν ῥήματι probably describes the substance that bathes those who receive this bath: they receive “the water bath in the word,” which is the gospel. Christ died, then, to sanctify the church by cleansing it with a water bath in the gospel.

To summarize, in the purpose clause contained in 5:26, Paul begins to digress from his instructions to husbands into a description of why Christ has showed his love for the church by giving his life for it. He did this to cleanse the people who would make up the church from their sin and to set them apart as God’s special people. This cleansing, sanctifying action was applied to them when they were washed in the verbal proclamation of the gospel, that is, when they heard the gospel preached, believed it, and were sealed as God’s special people by the Holy Spirit (cf. 1:13–14).

[5:27] If the imagery of a bridal bath lies somewhere in the background in 5:26, which seems likely (pace Robinson 1904: 207), then it continues here in the second purpose clause, where Paul states that Christ has sanctified the church in order to present it to himself as “brilliant” (ἔνδοξος, endoxos; BDAG 332). The church is pictured as a young bride of dazzling beauty. Her youth is evident from her unwrinkled skin, and her skin is unblemished as a result both of her youth and of the bridal bath she has just taken.[37] Since the term ἔνδοξος can describe resplendent clothing (Luke 7:25), Paul was probably thinking of the especially beautiful garments that a bride might wear on the day of her wedding.

The whole image is reminiscent of the elaborate toilette for both bride and groom that accompanied ancient weddings in Greek and Roman cultures. In the Greek world, bride and groom were given baths prior to the public parts of the wedding, and these baths were not merely ritual in nature. They also performed the practical function of cleaning the bride and groom so that they might look and smell their best (Oakley and Sinos 1993: 15). Although the ritual elements of the bath are not clear for the Roman world, both bride and groom nevertheless were carefully groomed and dressed (and it is difficult to imagine that they did not bathe). In both cultures, a large entourage of the bride’s family and friends helped her arrange her hair and get dressed in special—often colorful—garments, shoes, jewels, a veil, and a crown (Treggiari 1991: 163; Oakley and Sinos 1993: 16–21). In Hellenistic Judaism, the basic customs surrounding the bride’s preparation seem to have been the same: a careful toilette with help from the family, beautiful clothing—Aseneth’s wedding gown was “like lightning in appearance”—and washing in water (Jos. Asen. 18 [OTP 2:231–32]).

The difference here is the unusual picture of the groom bathing the bride (Eph. 5:26) and presenting her in all her splendor to himself (v. 27). The metaphor has taken this turn because the picture of a typical wedding has merged with the imagery of Ezek. 16:8–14. There God imagines Israel as his young bride, whom he has bathed, cleansed, anointed, and clothed in finery and jewels. Here in Ephesians, Christ takes the place of God in that imagery, and the church fills the place of Israel. Again, however, Paul breaks the boundary of a traditional image. In Ezek. 16 the imagery of the bride is part of a prophecy against Israel for its unfaithfulness to God: once made beautiful by God, Israel had become a prostitute through its promiscuous alliances with other nations and their gods. Paul’s image runs in the opposite direction: those who comprise the church were once stained, but through the death of Christ and the preaching of the gospel, Christ has cleansed them and set them apart for himself, just as a young and dazzlingly beautiful bride, in all her finery, is presented to the groom.

The final clause shows that Paul thought of this imagery in moral terms. The church is “brilliant” and without “blemish or wrinkle or any such things” in the sense that it is “holy and blameless.” Although the holiness and blamelessness of the church is an established reality through the death of Christ and the church’s response to the gospel, Paul also thinks of this reality as lived out in the day-to-day conduct of those who comprise the church. The phrase “holy and blameless,” therefore, recalls 1:4, where Paul has said that God chose his people so that they might be “holy and blameless before him in love” (see the notes on that passage). Implicit in this claim that the church is the resplendent bride of Christ, then, is a call to live in a way that is consistent with this status.

[5:28] The practical aspect of the imagery now becomes explicit again as Paul moves out of his reflection on the relationship between Christ and the church and back to the advice on marriage that has prompted it. The οὕτως (houtōs, so) points backward to the manner of Christ’s love for the church as Paul has just described it in 5:25–27,[﻿38] and Paul restates what he said in 5:25, but more emphatically and with an added motivation.

The greater emphasis comes with the way Paul states the obligation of husbands. In 5:25 he has merely said they are to love their wives, but here he strengthens the element of duty involved in this admonition: they “are obligated” (ὀφείλουσιν, opheilousin) to love their wives. The addition of the reflexive pronoun ἑαυτῶν (heautōn, their own) corresponds to the use of the adjective ἰδίοις in 5:22: just as wives are to submit to their own husbands, so here husbands are to love their own wives. Both terms highlight the exclusive nature of the relationship between husbands and wives: they are to have a level of commitment to each other that is qualitatively different from their commitments to other men and women.

The addition of ἑαυτῶν also prepares the way for the new thought that comes next. Husbands are to love their own wives as their own bodies. Paul backs up this admonition with a pithy saying that shifts to the singular and contains no formal grammatical connection to the surrounding material: “The one who loves his own wife loves himself.” Some interpreters have seen here an allusion to Lev. 19:18, which urges each Israelite to “love your neighbor as yourself [ὡς σεαυτόν, hōs seauton].” Paul does seem to recall that command in 5:33, but here the thought is somewhat different. Leviticus 19:18 speaks of loving one’s neighbor in the same way that one loves oneself, but here Paul speaks of the husband loving his wife because she is himself.

To us this may sound odd, but it probably would not have puzzled Paul’s readers. Some of them, like Paul, knew that Gen. 2:24 spoke of husband and wife as “one flesh” (Eph. 5:31; cf. 1 Cor. 6:16; Mark 10:7–8; Matt. 19:5–6). In addition, many of them probably accepted the widely dispersed notion in antiquity that husband and wife shared a close, even organic, unity with each other (Xenophon, Oec. 10.4; Musonius Rufus XIIIa [Lutz 1947: 88–89, lines 13–14]; XIV [Lutz 1947: 94–95, lines 8–9]; Plutarch, Conj. praec. 140f, 142f, 143a).

[5:29–30] Paul next explains (γάρ, gar, for) the practical implications of this common assumption: husbands are to care for their wives physically and emotionally as well as, or better than, they care for themselves. Hate and love are often contrasted in the NT as polar opposites (Matt. 6:24; Luke 16:13; John 12:25; Rom. 9:13), and although love is not an explicit member of Paul’s contrast here, it is implied by the use of “love” nearby, in Eph. 5:25, 28. The terms ἐκτρέφει (ektrephei, care for) and θάλπει (thalpei, cherish), then, describe in practical terms what love involves. These two terms were commonly used to describe the physical nurture and emotional warmth that one person gives to another, whether a child (1 Thess. 2:7; Eph. 6:4), a spouse (CPR 1.30 frag. 2, line 20), or a lover (Theocritus, Id. 14.38). Paul wants the husbands among his readers to understand that loving their wives means taking care of them both physically and emotionally.

In 5:29c–30 Paul moves back to the analogy between the husband’s love for his wife and Christ’s love for the church that has grounded his admonition to the husband in 5:25 and 28, and he takes that analogy to a deeper level. Believers, he says, are members of Christ’s body (cf. 1 Cor. 6:15), so Christ cares for them in the way that anyone would care for his own body. Here he recalls his use of the term “body” earlier in the letter to describe Christ’s protection of the church from its enemies (Eph. 1:20–23) and Christ’s provision, lovingly given to the church, of everything necessary for its nourishment and support (4:7–16, esp. vv. 15–16). Husband and wife, likewise, are one body, and the husband should provide physical and emotional support to his wife, who is his body, self, and flesh, just as Christ cares for his body, the church.

[5:31–32] Paul now uses the language of Gen. 2:24 to support what he has just said in Eph. 5:29–30.[39] He uses no introductory quotation formula (cf. 1:22; 2:17; 4:25–26; 6:2), but Gen. 2:24 was cited frequently enough in early Christian discussions of sex and marriage that he can safely assume that his readers will understand the source of his words (1 Cor. 6:16; Mark 10:7–8; Matt. 19:5–6).

His quotation differs from the LXX in two ways. First, Paul omits αὐτοῦ (autou, his) both after πατέρα (patera, father) and after μητέρα (mētera, mother). This condenses the quotation but does not alter its meaning (cf. Matt. 19:5 with Mark 10:7). Second, he begins the quotation with ἀντὶ τούτου (anti toutou, on account of this) instead of ἕνεκεν τούτου (heneken toutou, on account of this).[40]

This second change is important, not because it alters the meaning, but because the change shows that Paul was probably aware of the wording of this opening phrase enough to alter it slightly. He did not include the opening phrase unthinkingly simply because it belonged to the first part of the quotation he wanted to use. Rather, he viewed the phrase as a fitting way of connecting the substance of the quotation with his previous argument. In other words, we should think of ἀντὶ τούτου as having true argumentative force: “on account of” something Paul has just said, “a man will leave his father and his mother.”

What part of his previous discourse was he trying to support? Was he supporting the idea that Christ and the church are one body? That husband and wife are one body? Both ideas? On one hand, the quotation comes directly after Paul’s statement that Christ nourishes and cares for the church as his body (5:29b–30), and Paul concludes the quotation by saying that he is applying it to Christ and the church (5:32b). It might seem reasonable to think, then, that the quotation demonstrates the unity of Christ with the church. On the other hand, the quotation itself concerns the union of a man and a woman in marriage, and the larger context in which Paul uses it argues that a husband should love his wife as he loves himself. In such a context, it would seem strange if the quotation does not refer to the unity of husband and wife in marriage.

The quotation probably refers to both themes, but primarily to the unity of Christ and the church. The primacy of the Christ-church reference is visible in three aspects of the quotation and its context. First, Paul explicitly says that he intends the quotation to apply to Christ and to the church (v. 32).[41] Second, the phrase “because of this” (ἀντὶ τούτου), which opens the quotation, refers most naturally to the preceding statements about Christ’s care for his church body (vv. 29c–30). Third, the term πλήν (plēn, nevertheless) that begins 5:33 pulls the reader back to the train of thought Paul had been developing before he began to digress about Christ’s relationship to the church in 5:29c. This means that the quotation and its explanation in 5:31–32 are part of the digression on the relationship between Christ and the church.

If this is correct, then, as surprising as it may seem, Paul is saying in 5:31 that God has instituted marriage “because” the church is Christ’s body. This probably means that the union of husband and wife in “one flesh” was originally intended to prefigure and to illustrate the union that Christ now has with the church. This is something that could become clear only after Christ had died to create the church in its new, multiethnic form (2:14–15; 3:8–11), and this is why it is a μυστήριον (mystērion, mystery): a truth that could be known only through God’s gracious revelation of it (1:9; 3:3–4, 9; 6:19). It is a μέγα (mega, great) mystery because it is unusually mysterious. The adjective μέγας, says I. Marshall (1999: 522n63), “appears to express the greatness of the degree to which the thing or person is what it is; a ‘great mystery’ is especially mysterious.”[42] The application of Gen. 2:24 to the union of Christ with the church would be nonsensical apart from a special revelation from God that tells of this application.

This especially mysterious nature of Paul’s interpretation probably explains the syntax at the beginning of 5:32. Many commentators think that when Paul uses the phrase ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω (egō de legō, but I am speaking) in this verse he is contrasting his own interpretation of Gen. 2:24 with other interpretations (e.g., Ellicott 1859: 136; Lincoln 1990: 382; Merz 2000: 135–36; cf. Schnackenburg 1991: 255; Sampley 1971: 89). If that were correct, however, he would have provided more guidance for his readers about precisely what interpretations of Gen. 2:24 he was reacting against.[43] It is more likely, then, that the conjunction δέ (de, but) in this phrase sets up a contrast between Paul’s recognition that his interpretation is surprising and his determination, nevertheless, to reveal it to his readers. If this is correct, then the phrase “this mystery” does not point back to Gen. 2:24 but forward to Paul’s interpretation of it. He says in effect, “The mystery I am about to describe is especially mysterious, but I am going to say it anyway: when I refer to the well-known establishment of marriage in the book of Genesis, I am talking about Christ and the church.”

Paul does not deny that the common reading of Gen. 2:24 is true. He has built his argument in 1 Cor. 6:16 on that common reading, and as his switch from “body” to “flesh” terminology in 5:29a shows, part of his admonition to husbands to love their wives is also built on it. Genesis 2:24 also supports the union of Christ with the church, however, and this unity has not only been an important, independent theme in the letter so far (2:5–6, 20; 4:11–16), but it has also served as an example for husbands to follow in the love they show to their wives (5:23, 25, 28).

[5:33] Paul jerks the discussion back on track with the word πλήν (plēn), meaning “in any case” and often used, especially in Paul’s writings, for “breaking off a discussion and emphasizing what is important” (BDAG 826; cf. 1 Cor. 11:11; Phil. 3:16; 4:14; pace, e.g., Eadie 1883: 435). Here he returns to his main concern throughout the section—the practical relationship between husband and wife—and offers a concluding summary of his admonitions to both. The emphatic phrase ὑμεῖς οἱ καθ᾿ ἕνα (hymeis hoi kath’ hena) points a finger directly at each husband among Paul’s readers and then underlines this individual appeal with the word ἕκαστος (hekastos, each). The result is impossible to translate literally, but effectively says, “You—every single one of you.”[44] The admonition Paul gives is a summary of what he has said in 5:28–29b, strengthened by the reminder of the common reading of Gen. 2:24. Each husband must love his own wife as himself because she is one flesh with him. The way Paul puts his admonition recalls Lev. 19:18, which is also framed in the singular and also compares love for the other with love for oneself. If this recollection is intentional, however, then Lev. 19:18 is redefined by the unique sense in which the wife is the husband’s neighbor. She is one flesh with him and thus the closest possible neighbor. Perhaps this is why Paul emphasizes that the husband is to love “his own [ἑαυτοῦ, heautou] wife” as himself. Although believers should understand Lev. 19:18 to refer to their love for every neighbor, including their enemies (Mark 12:31, 33; Matt. 19:19; 22:39; Luke 10:27; Gal. 5:14; Rom. 13:9; James 2:8), the husband’s love for his wife is to have a unique quality, reflecting the truth expressed in Gen. 2:24—that he and his wife are “one flesh.”

The wife, for her part (δέ, de), “should fear” (ἵνα φοβῆται, hina phobētai) her husband. Using ἵνα and the subjunctive to express an imperative is characteristic of the Greek in Hellenistic Jewish texts (e.g., 2 Macc 1:9), including the NT (Mark 5:23; 10:51; Matt. 20:33), and it shows up several times in the Pauline corpus (1 Cor. 7:29; Gal. 2:10; 2 Cor. 8:7).[45] In the NT it often carries a softer, more respectful nuance than the simple imperative. When Jesus asked blind Bartimaeus what he wanted him to do, “The blind man said, ‘My rabbi, that I might see again’ [ἵνα ἀναβλέψω, hina anablepsō]’” (Mark 10:51; cf. Matt. 20:33). This was a softer way of saying, “Give me back my sight!” Similarly, James, Cephas, and John did not order Paul and Barnabas around when they decide how to divide their missionary labor, but they “asked only one thing, that we remember [ἵνα μνημονεύωμεν, hina mnēmoneuōmen] the poor” (Gal. 2:10 NRSV). The same tone is probably what Paul intended here, particularly since he has just used the proper imperative mood in the previous clause.[46] The husband is told emphatically to love his wife, but the command to the wife has a milder tone: she “should fear her husband” (Barth 1974: 648).

The softer tone is consistent with the more reserved tone of the command for wives to submit to husbands in 5:22 and 24, where in each case the verb has to be supplied and the imperative is implied rather than stated. This does not remove the reality of the imperative—it is certainly present—but it is perhaps a subtle recognition that in terms of the balance of power bestowed by Greco-Roman society on husband and wife, the wife had the more difficult role. In a society in which women had less say over who they married than men, and less power within the relationship once the marriage had taken place, it was important for a household code that had been transformed by the gospel not to be heavy-handed in its instructions to the less-powerful partner.

The softer tone may be especially appropriate here, since Paul calls on the wife to “fear” (φοβέω, phobeō) her husband. This recalls his instructions to all believers in 5:21, that they should submit to one another “in the fear [φόβῳ, phobō] of Christ.” Just as fear there was something more than respect and less than terror, and was tempered by Paul’s lavish references to Christ’s love (see the comment on that verse), so here “fear” recognizes the authoritative role of the husband, but also the way in which Paul has tempered that role with extensive instruction to the husband to love his wife. But what if the wife is married to someone who does not love her as Christ loved the church? Perhaps the softness of the imperative is a recognition that the wife’s obedience to Paul’s instructions will often involve complexities introduced by the inevitable mixture of her husband’s sinfulness with his position of authoritative head.

Summary

In 5:21–33 Paul continues his positive instruction about how believers ought to live carefully and wisely in the present evil time (5:15–16), doing the Lord’s will (5:17), growing in maturity, and living in the Spirit (5:18). In this passage, he begins to focus on how this way of living looks when it is applied to the makeup of the traditional Greco-Roman household. He first addresses the duties of wives and husbands to each other, and his purpose in this description is twofold. First, he offers what initially sounds like the culturally traditional advice that the wife should submit to her husband and that the husband is the head of his wife. In the same breath, however, he redefines the traditional expectations about the husband’s authority so that his power is used entirely for his wife’s benefit, even if loving her in this way should involve laying down his life for her.

Second, Paul wanted to give an account of the close, loving relationship between Christ and the church. Paul’s prayer report in 1:19–23 has included the petition that his readers might understand how God, in Christ, has put his great power into effect on behalf of the church. Now, in a digression from the practical conduct of wife and husband in marriage, he elaborates on how God has done this. Christ showed his love for the church by dying for it, cleansing it of sin, and separating it from the rest of the world, just as a bride is cleansed and made beautiful before her wedding. Surpisingly, says Paul, this is why God has instituted marriage in the first place. On the human level it illustrates the extent of God’s great love for his people in Christ.



Additional Notes

5:22. Two very early Alexandrian manuscripts (𝔓46, B) have no verb in this verse and expect the reader mentally to supply some form of the verb ὑποτάσσω (cf. vv. 21, 24) to fill out the meaning. According to Jerome, writing from Bethlehem in the late fourth century, the verb was missing “in the Greek codices” (Heine 2002: 233). In other Alexandrian manuscripts (א, A, I, P, 6, 33, 81, 104, 256), however, the verb ὑποτασσέσθωσαν appears after ἀνδράσιν, so the text reads αἱ γυναῖκες τοῖς ἰδίοις ἀνδράσιν ὑποτασσέσθωσαν ὡς τῷ κυρίω (Let wives submit themselves to their own husbands as to the Lord). In a few Western witnesses ὑποτάσσεσθε appears after γυναῖκες, just as it does in Col. 3:18 (D, F, G, and one manuscript of the Old Latin). In some late manuscripts of an independent text type (dating from the ninth to the fourteenth centuries), the same form appears after ἀνδράσιν (075, 0150, 424, 1852, 1912, 2200). In one late Alexandrian manuscript (Ψ), the form ὑποτασσέσθωσαν appears after γυναῖκες.

The variations are not entirely insignificant for the meaning of the passage. Without the verb, v. 22 is more closely connected to v. 21, and if Paul wrote the third-person-plural form of the verb, he is no longer addressing wives directly but simply telling his readers generally that wives must submit to their husbands (cf. 1 Cor. 14:34; 1 Clem. 21.6; Ign. Pol. 5.1; Pol. Phil. 4.2).

It is likely, however, that Paul did not supply a verb for verse 22. This supposition makes it easy to account for the presence of a verb in various forms and various places among the witnesses. When 5:22–6:9 began to be read aloud in churches as a separate passage, it would be necessary to supply a verb somewhere in the first sentence to make the reading intelligible (Robinson 1904: 204), and it is understandable that the form of the verb and its precise location would vary as the text was read in slightly different ways in different places. It is not easy, however, to account for the omission of the verb if Paul had originally supplied it.

Among the witnesses who supply a verb, moreover, the best attested form is the third-person imperative, and yet if Paul had written this, it is strange that he then proceeded to address children and slaves directly in the second person (6:1, 5). Although the manuscripts without the verb are few and from a single tradition (the Alexandrian), they nevertheless are early and, in view of the other considerations, probably preserve the original text.

5:27. I take the phrase ἵνα παραστήσῃ to refer to a reality that already exists (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 377; Schnackenburg 1991: 250–51; Best 1998: 545–46) rather than to a future reality (e.g., Ellicott 1859: 131; Eadie 1883: 422–23; O’Brien 1999: 425). This means that Paul uses παρίστημι differently here than he has used it in the betrothal imagery of 2 Cor. 11:2, where he is the chief actor and, in this role, envisions himself presenting the Corinthian congregation to Christ in marriage as a “pure virgin” unsullied by false teaching (11:4). That is a future reference in step with Paul’s desire expressed elsewhere that the congregations under his oversight arrive at the final day “holy” and “blameless” (1 Thess. 3:13; 5:23; Col. 1:22) and that he be able to present them to the Lord Jesus on that day as his “crown” (1 Thess. 2:19; Phil. 4:1; cf. Rom. 15:16).

In the difference between 2 Cor. 11:2 and Eph. 5:27, however, there is no reason to see a sign that Ephesians is pseudepigraphic. Even in the undisputed letters the image can vary: in 2 Cor. 4:14 God “will present” (παραστήσει) both Paul and the Corinthian congregation to himself at the time of the resurrection, and in Rom. 12:1 the Roman believers are to “present” (παραστῆσαι) their bodies as sacrifices to God in the present (cf. 2 Tim. 2:15). It is certainly within the bounds of Paul’s previous use of this image, therefore, for him to speak here of Christ presenting the church to himself in the present as a bride that is already cleansed, holy, and blameless.

5:30. In a number of manuscripts—across the Alexandrian (Ψ, 104), Western (D, F, G; cf. 1912), and Byzantine traditions (most)—the phrase ἐκ τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐκ τῶν ὀστέων αὐτοῦ (from his flesh, and from his bones) follows Paul’s comment that μέλη ἐσμὲν τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ (we are parts of his body). The phrase is clearly an allusion to Gen. 2:23 (with the order of “flesh” and “bones” reversed), but its meaning is obscure. Does it mean that Christ nourishes believers through the Lord’s Supper (Calvin 1965: 209)? That he is united with them in their humanity (Ellicott 1859: 134–35)?[47] No explanation is convincing. From one way of looking at the problem, this might reduce the probability that a scribe added the phrase. Scribes tended to clarify rather than cloud the text (Muddiman 2001: 268; Hoehner 2002: 769–70).

The phrase is missing, however, from an impressive array of Alexandrian uncials as well as from several valuable minuscules with Alexandrian leanings (e.g., 𝔓46, א, A, B, 048, 6, 33, 81, 1739). It is true that this limits the absence of the phrase primarily to one text type (Hoehner 2002: 769n3), but the antiquity and conservative nature of these manuscripts outweighs the value of the diversity of manuscripts with the longer reading. The phrase probably represents an unskillful attempt to smooth what is otherwise an abrupt transition from the thought that believers are members of Christ’s body (v. 30) to the interpretation of Gen. 2:24 in terms of Christ and the church in (vv. 31–32).





2. Children and Parents (6:1–4)

Paul turns next to the relationship between children and parents, the second of the three major topics of Hellenistic philosophical reflection on the ordering of the household and a common topic of moral discussion in antiquity generally. Once again, he addresses children and fathers directly, speaking to the subordinate member of the pair first, and probably imagining that both groups are gathered within a house with other believers for worship, listening to his letter as it is read aloud (cf. 5:19–20).

Whereas his instruction to husbands has been longer than his instruction to wives, however, here the subordinate members of the pair—children—receive most of the attention. Paul urges children to obey their parents and gives three reasons why they should do this. First, it is conduct expected of those who have been incorporated into the Lord through their faith in the gospel. Second, it is “right,” by which Paul probably means that obedience to parents is widely acknowledged to be fair and proper. Third, the Scriptures both command it and attach a promise to the command—the first promise in the Mosaic law that is attached to a specific command. Paul is primarily concerned with this third reason for obedience to parents: the Scriptures promise that, generally speaking, children who obey their parents will live successful and long lives.

When Paul turns to parents, he narrows his focus to fathers. Although children must obey both parents (6:1–2), Paul implicitly recognizes that as the dominant person in the ancient household, fathers need special instruction on how to use their positions of authority. Just as he did with husbands, Paul restricts the father’s use of his authority to benevolent and positive purposes in the life of the one under his authority. Fathers should lovingly rear their children in the traditions of the faith, not driving them to anger, but warning them away from harmful influences (cf. 4:14) and teaching them to be disciples of the living Christ (cf. 4:20).



Exegesis and Exposition

1Children, obey your parents ⌜in the Lord⌝, for this is right. 2Honor your father and mother, which is the first commandment with a promise, 3that it might go well with you and you will live long on the earth.

4And fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

[6:1] Just as in his treatment of wives and husbands and slaves and masters, Paul first addresses the subordinate members of the pair, and does so directly, as if they are present in the worshiping assembly where he expects this letter to be read. The tone of the command to children is slightly stronger than it was with wives: instead of implying a passive form of the verb ὑποτάσσω (hypotassō, submit) in his command, as he did with wives (5:22, 24b), he explicitly expresses an active form of the verb ὑπακούω (hypakouō, obey). The emphasis on the voluntary element in the submission of wives, then, is missing from the command to children. “Childen,” he instructs them, “obey your parents” (cf. 6:5).

In the Greco-Roman world, the duties of children toward their parents included love (Cicero, Part. or. 25.88; Seneca, Ben. 3.1.5; Chaeremon in Stobaeus, Flor. 79; Balla 2003: 66, 68–69), honor (Diogenes Laertius, Vit. phil. 7.120; Seneca, Ben. 3.1.5; Balla 2003: 63), providing for them in old age, burying them, and venerating them after death (Balla 2003: 64–68). All these activities were part of pietas, the virtue that lay “at the core of the Romans’ ideal of family relations” and that involved the heartfelt fulfillment of one’s duty toward the gods, country, and family (Saller 1994: 105). A person’s highest moral duty, said Cicero (Off. 1.17.58, in Balla 2003: 64), was first to one’s country and then to one’s parents, “for their services have laid us under the heaviest obligation.”

Obedience was a critical element in these obligations, although there were unusual circumstances in which disobedience was thought to be understandable (Saller 1994: 105–14; Balla 2003: 73–76). Musonius Rufus’s first-century discourse on whether “obedience to parents in all things” (πάντα πειστέον τοῖς γονεῦσιν, panta peisteon tois goneusin) is necessary demonstrates the approach of most people: obedience to parents was the norm, and any exceptions to it needed thoughtful discussion.

Hellenistic Jewish literature takes a similar approach. Children were expected not only to provide for their elderly parents and see to their burial (Sir. 3:12; Sib. Or. 2.159–60; Philo, Decalogue 116; Tob. 4:3–4; Balla 2003: 94–96), but also to honor them next only to God (Philo, Decalogue 106–7; Sib. Or. 2.59–60; Ps.-Phoc. 8; Jub. 7.20; Balla 2003: 86–91), speak respectfully to them (Exod. 21:16 LXX [21:17 MT, Eng.]; Philo, Spec. Laws 2.248; Sir. 3:8; Sib. Or. 2.275–76; Balla 2003: 92), and provide for them in old age (Tob. 4:3; Josephus, Ant. 4.261; Balla 2003: 95; cf. 1 Tim. 5:4, 8; Matt. 15:3–8).

Just as in the Greco-Roman world generally, obedience to parents was a critical element in fulfilling one’s duty toward them (Sir. 7:23; Jub. 39.6; Prov. 1:8–9; 3:11–12; 17:25; 2 Tim. 1:5; 3:15; Heb. 12:6–7; Josephus, Ag. Ap. 2.204; T. Reu. 3.8; T. Jud. 1.4; Balla 2003: 83–84, 93), although here too obedience to parents was sometimes qualified. It seems to have been assumed that where a conflict arose between obedience to parents and what is “just and profitable” (Philo, Spec. Laws 2.236), including obedience to God (Josephus, Ag. Ap. 2.206), it would be necessary to disobey the teaching or wishes of one’s parents (Balla 2003: 104–9).

Although in the closely parallel passage in Col. 3:20 Paul tells children to obey their parents “in all things” (κατὰ πάντα, kata panta), and here he simply tells them to obey their parents with no qualifications, it seems unlikely that he would have differed from his culture in advocating unlimited obedience to parents. As with his admonition to wives in 5:24 to submit to their husbands “in everything” (ἐν παντί, en panti), his emphasis lies on submission to those in authority. Since he is being concise, and since he assumes an ideal situation in which Christian parents are instructing Christian children (6:4), he does not say what he probably assumed his readers knew: there are unusual circumstances in which this command cannot be strictly obeyed.

Paul describes three motivations for his command, the first two of which occur in this first sentence of the new section. First, children are to obey their parents ἐν κυρίῳ (en kyriō, in the Lord). These words are missing from several important manuscripts in both the Alexandrian and Western traditions, but as the additional note explains, the argument for including them is more persuasive than the case for their omission. Throughout Ephesians the phrase ἐν κυρίῳ has referred to the incorporation of believers into Christ: they grow up into a holy temple “in the Lord” (2:21); Paul is a prisoner “in the Lord” (4:1); Paul gives his readers ethical instruction “in the Lord” (4:17); and when they believed the gospel, Paul’s readers became light “in the Lord” (5:8). Here too, then, Paul must be talking about conduct that he expects of children because they are “in the Lord.” Because they have been incorporated into Christ by faith (1:13), they should obey their parents.

Second, children should obey their parents because it is “right” (δίκαιος, dikaios) to do so. The adjective δίκαιος refers to conduct widely acknowledged to be fair and proper (Sir. 10:23; Phil. 4:8; Matt. 20:4; Luke 12:57; BDAG 247), and this statement probably reflects Paul’s understanding that obedience to parents was a nearly universally acknowledged virtue. The philosopher Pythagoras (sixth cent. BC), for example, apparently considered gratitude, love, and obedience to parents to be “right” (δίκαιος), in part because parents are “our earliest and greatest benefactors” (Iamblichus, Vita Pythagorae 38–40; G. Clark 1989: 15).[1] It was only fair that children should be dutiful toward their parents since their parents had given them life and reared them.

For Paul, obedience to parents was basic to the functioning of society, and the widespread neglect of this obvious principle of conduct was a sign of the moral chaos into which the world had degenerated in “the last days” (Rom. 1:30; 2 Tim. 3:2). Believing children, however, should have nothing to do with this trend: their conduct with respect to their parents should match what everyone recognizes to be right.

[6:2–3] Third, Paul believes that children should obey their parents because the Decalogue mandates it in what ancient Jews numbered as the fifth commandment (Philo, Decalogue 106).[2] No formula introduces Paul’s quotation of this commandment, and no conjunction joins it to the admonition it is intended to support. Paul simply states the commandment, probably a sign that he thinks it is well known to his readers and that it is self-evidently authoritative.

First-century Jewish interpreters frequently pointed out the important place that the commandment occupies within the Decalogue and the implications this has for the immense stature of parents. It sits on the “borderline,” Philo says, “between the two sets of five,” the first set governing one’s relationship with God, and the second set governing one’s relationship with people. This is because “parents by their nature stand on the borderline between the mortal and the immortal side of existence.” Like other human beings, they are mortal, but because they give rise to a succession of other human beings, they share in God’s immortality (Decalogue 106–7; cf. 119–20; Spec. Laws 2.224–25; Josephus, Ag. Ap. 2.206; Barclay 2007: 288–89).

Paul draws no parallels between parents and God. Instead, he explains the importance of the command from the promise that is attached to it and thus from the blessing that comes to children who obey it. Its importance is clear, he reasons, from its status as “the first command [ἐντολὴ πρώτη, entolē prōtē] with a promise.”

This statement has puzzled interpreters for centuries because at first it seems to be incorrect. As Origen had already noticed in the third century, there is a promise attached to the second commandment, which forbids making idols. There we read that God will both punish those who hate him and show mercy to those who keep his decrees (Exod. 20:4–6; Heine 2002: 245). How, then, can Paul say that the fifth commandment is the first commandment with a promise attached?

Interpreters have answered this question in a wide variety of ways. Some argue that the word πρώτη carries a meaning other than its usual one of “first in sequence.” Perhaps obedience to parents is the “weightiest” commandment with a promise (Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 95), or a “pre-eminent” commandment with a promise (Best 1998: 566–67), or the “most important” of the commandments that promise something (Muddiman 2001: 275), or “a commandment of great importance, with a promise attached” (BDAG 893).

Against all these interpretations, however, must stand the normal meaning of the term πρώτη. It is true that in the Gospels Jesus can speak of “the great and most important [πρώτη] commandment” (Matt. 22:38; cf. Mark 12:28–29), but even here πρώτη means “first in a sequence of two commandments ordered according to their importance” (Matt. 22:39; Mark 12:31). “The πρώτη commandment with a promise” most naturally means the first of a series of commands that has a promise (Meyer 1880: 315).

Three other explanations of the phrase start with the assumption that this is what it means. One of these explanations organizes the Decalogue into two parts, the first part governing duties to God, and the second part treating duties toward other human beings. The command to honor one’s parents, then, would be the “first” commandment of the Decalogue’s second part (Schnackenburg 1991: 261–62). There is no clear evidence, however, that first-century Jews organized the commandments this way. Philo describes the commands of the Decalogue that deal with God as more important than the commands that deal with mortals, and he considers the command to obey one’s parents to “be concerned with mortal things” (Spec. Laws 2.261, trans. Colson 1939; Schnackenburg 1991: 262). Elsewhere, however, he places obedience to parents “on the border-line between the two sets of five” (Decalogue 106, trans. Colson 1939) and considers it the last of the commands about one’s duty to God (Decalogue 51, 121; cf. Best 1998: 556). If we can tell anything from Rom. 13:9 about how Paul organized the Decalogue in his own thinking, he also considered obedience to parents as the last of the first five commands, not as the first command of the second set of five.

A second explanation says that Paul must have thought Exod. 20:12 to be the first commandment that children learned as they were growing up (Abbott 1897: 177, although hesitantly). If Paul had meant this, however, he would have expressed himself more clearly. It would have been simple to write, “This is the first commandment that you learned with a promise.”[3]

The third among those explanations that assign πρώτη its most obvious meaning in this context, then, is probably correct, and most interpreters down through the centuries have adopted it. If Paul is thinking of the legislation that God gave to Moses for Israel on Sinai, and not of commandments that precede the Mosaic law, then the command to obey one’s parents turns out to be the first commandment with a promise attached specifically to it. The second commandment certainly does precede the fifth commandment and does have a promise associated with it, but the promise is general in nature and applicable to much more than the second commandment: God punishes those who reject him and shows love to those who love him and keep his commandments (Calvin 1965: 213; Ellicott 1859: 138; Meyer 1880: 314; Eadie 1883: 439–40; Robinson 1904: 210; Aletti 2001: 295n98; Lincoln 1990: 404; cf. Moritz 1996a: 156, 172–74). Paul expresses the great importance of the command to obey one’s parents by reminding the children in his audience that this is the first command in the Mosaic law specifically attached to a promise.

The promise given to those who obey the command has two parts: “that it might go well with you” and “that you will live long on τῆς γῆς [tēs gēs, the earth].”[4] The first part of this promise is identical to the fifth commandment as it appears in the LXX of both Exod. 20:12 and Deut. 5:16.﻿[5]﻿ The second part of the promise in Eph. 6:3 drops the further definition of τῆς γῆς in both OT texts as “the land that the Lord your God is giving to you.” This has the effect of changing the specific reference to the land of Canaan in the commandment into a reference to long life in general (cf. Philo, Spec. Laws 2.261), thus making a commandment once pertinent only to the nation of Israel into a precept by which “the one new man” drawn from both Jews and Gentiles should live.

In Eph. 2:15, when Paul speaks of “setting aside the law of commandments [promulgated] in [the form of] decrees,” therefore, he does not mean that the Mosaic law is no longer useful for guiding the conduct of God’s people, nor do we find here that it is now useful for God’s people in the same way that it once was. Rather, parts of the Mosaic law have been absorbed into the ethical teaching for the newly formed people of God, and they have been changed to make them universal in nature.

Much ink has flowed over the question of how the promise that obedient children will live long on the earth should be understood. Clearly, every obedient child does not have a long life. Some interpreters, therefore, have thought that the reference is to eternal life (Jerome [Heine 2002: 246–47]; Muddiman 2001: 274), others that the whole people as much as the individual is in view (De Wette 1843: 154), and still others that the reference to long life must be taken literally but represents a regressive and shallow moral perspective (Best 1998: 568).

Perhaps the most sensible comment on the issue came from Alford (1857: 138) long ago: “When we remember that the persons addressed are τὰ τέκνα, we must not depart from the simplest sense of the words.” Paul envisioned an audience of children gathered in the house churches where this letter would be read aloud and whom he addresses directly. He therefore avoided subtleties and simply recalled to their minds a commandment that many of them had probably learned by heart. Ephesians was written in a world where between 39 and 50 percent of children died before their tenth birthday (Saller 1994: 25), rates so high that excessive mourning over a child’s death was thought to be in poor taste (Dixon 1992: 99, 107). In such a situation, Paul probably expected that the same parents who taught their children the fifth commandment had already addressed the probing questions children often ask about how such ethical principles apply to practical, everyday life. Everyone would be aware that many well-behaved children succumb to untimely deaths, but most people would also know that, provided they escaped disease and accident, children who took to heart the wisdom of those who cared for them had a better chance of doing well and living long than those who despised their parent’s instruction (Prov. 15:5; 20:20; 30:17; cf. Prov. 6:20–22; 13:1; 23:22).

[6:4] Just as in his treatment of wives and husbands (5:22–33), so here in his treatment of children and parents, Paul instructs the male head of the household to conduct himself toward those under his authority with restraint and for their good. The καί (kai, also) with which the sentence begins stresses the mutuality of the relationship between children and parents: in the same way that children have a responsibility to obey their parents, fathers “also” have a responsibility to use their authority for the good of their children (Ellicott 1859: 139; Abbott 1897: 178; Haupt 1902a: 227; O’Brien 1999: 445).

Specifically, fathers are not to “provoke” their children “to anger” (παροργίζω, parorgizō), a verb that recalls the use of its corresponding noun in 4:26 (παροργισμός, parorgismos) and the command issued there not to let the sun set on one’s wrath.[6] There Paul was concerned with the bitterness and resentment that results from anger left to fester. Here he is probably also concerned with the smoldering anger that results from unreasonable parental demands and severe punishment (cf. Col. 3:21). Although it is possible to exaggerate the extent to which the father in ancient Roman households threw his weight around (Saller 1994: 133–53), by modern standards he was an extraordinarily powerful figure, with far-reaching legal authority over his children. The powerful father was also part of Greek and Jewish culture (Hoehner 2002: 794–96). Here Paul reins in this power, urging fathers not to abuse their authority by treating their children in harsh, unfair ways that create resentment and bitterness.

Instead of this, fathers are to “bring up” (ἐκτρέφω, ektrephō) their children in “the training [παιδεία, paideia] and instruction [νουθεσία, nouthesia] of the Lord.” Paul used the term ἐκτρέφω in 5:29 to refer to the loving care a husband should provide for his wife. In the LXX the term frequently refers simply to “rearing” children (e.g., 1 Kings 11:20; 12:8–10; 2 Kings 10:6; 2 Chron. 10:10; Isa. 23:4; Hos. 9:12; Zech. 10:9; 1 Esd. 4:16, 20; 1 Macc. 6:17; 2 Macc. 7:27). The “rearing” of children in the Jewish tradition included not only providing for their physical needs, but also showing them affection (2 Sam. 12:3 LXX), and especially teaching them the law of God (Deut. 6:6–7; 11:18–19; Josephus, Ag. Ap. 2.204; cf. 1.60; 2.173–74; Ant. 4.211; Barclay 2007: 287). Something similar to this last concern is Paul’s focus when he says that children should be reared in the παιδεία and νουθεσία of the Lord.

The term παιδεία had a broad range of meanings, from physical and mental training in the values of a particular culture (e.g., Plato, Resp. 2.376e; Pseudo-Plato, Def. 416; 4 Macc. 10:10; 13:22; 1 Tim. 3:16) to disciplinary punishment (e.g., 2 Esd. 7:26 LXX [Ezra 7:26 MT, Eng.]; 2 Macc. 6:12; 7:33).[7] In early Christian literature, even when the element of disciplinary punishment in παιδεία is emphasized, the educational value of the punishment, and so its inherently merciful quality, is also important (2 Tim. 3:16; Heb. 12:5–11; 1 Clem. 56.16).

The term νουθεσία could refer simply to “good counsel” (Aristophanes, Ran. 1009, trans. Henderson 2002), but closer to the time of Paul it was used with slightly more negative connotations. In the Wisdom of Solomon it means the “warning” (NRSV) God gave the wilderness generation of Israelites about their conduct when he sent serpents among them in response to their complaints against God and Moses (16:6; cf. Num. 21:5–7). Philo used it in the same way of the “admonition” God gave the Egyptians when he struck them with plagues (Moses 1.113, 119, trans. Colson 1939). The rod that Judah left with Tamar reminds Philo of “admonition” (νουθεσία), “chastening” (σωφρονισμός, sōphronismos), and “discipline” (παιδεία; Names 135, trans. Colson 1939). Paul, too, calls the scriptural record of God’s punishment of Israel’s idolatry at the time of the exodus a “warning” (νουθεσία) for the Corinthian believers (1 Cor. 10:11; cf. Titus 3:10).

Here in Eph. 6:4, where Paul both circumscribes the power of the father of the household and reminds him of his responsibilities, it is likely that νουθεσία has an admonitory, but not a punitive, nuance (cf. Schnackenburg 1991: 263). His use of the word is similar to that of Diodorus Siculus (first cent. BC), who describes how the Sicilian tyrant Dionysius sold the philosopher Plato into slavery for speaking candidly to him. Plato’s friends purchased his freedom and shipped him to Greece “with the friendly admonition [φιλικὴν νουθεσίαν, philikēn nouthesian] that a wise man should associate with tyrants either as little as possible [ἥκιστα, hēkista] or with the best grace possible [ἥδιστα, hēdista]” (Diodorus Siculus, Biblio. hist. 15.7.1, trans. C. Oldfather 1933–67).[8] Plato’s friends used a traditional aphorism as a well-intended “admonition” to Plato not to make the same serious mistake again.

The tradition that Paul wanted fathers to use in the education of their children comes from “the Lord” (κυρίου, kyriou), that is, the Lord Jesus Christ (cf. 5:20). The genitive noun κυρίου, then, is subjective, and Paul refers to the training and instruction that the Lord gives to children through the family father (Bertram, TDNT 5:624). Paul probably had especially in mind the sort of training and instruction about “the truth in Jesus” (4:21) that he had already mentioned in 4:20–24.

Summary

In 6:1–4 Paul continues his instruction on living wisely in evil days, doing the Lord’s will, growing in maturity, and living in the realm of the Spirit (5:15–18) with respect to one’s conduct in the household. In this paragraph he addresses the relationship between children and their parents, especially their fathers. He instructs children to obey their parents for three reasons: (1) it is required by their relationship with the Lord Jesus Christ; (2) it is universally recognized as the right thing to do; and (3) God has commanded it and has emphasized its importance, promising that, as a general rule, children who obey their parents will prosper. Fathers, for their part, should not use their authority over their children in ways that breed resentment but should instead instruct and admonish them with the teaching of Jesus.



Additional Note

6:1. The phrase ἐν κυρίῳ is absent from the important Alexandrian manuscript B and the Western trio D, F, and G. The manuscript support for including the phrase, however, is stronger. It includes the early Alexandrian witnesses 𝔓46, א, A, and Ψ; most Byzantine manuscripts; and 1912, which has Western affinities.

The strength of the external support for including the phrase has led most commentators to accept it (e.g., Meyer 1880: 311; Lincoln 1990: 395; Metzger 1994: 541–42; Hoehner 2002: 785–86n1). If it were a scribal gloss, they argue, it would have probably read ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ (5:22; 6:7) or would have been placed after δίκαιον (cf. Col. 3:20).

Best (1998) argues for omitting the phrase because the quotation of the commandment in 6:2 already implies the divine origin of the author’s instructions. There was no need, then, for the author to emphasize that obedience to parents was a duty “in the Lord.”

Redundancy is such a prominent stylistic feature of Ephesians, however, that a double reference to the divine origin of the idea of obedience to parents is not surprising. It seems best, then, to agree with the majority of commentators and accept the phrase as original on the basis of its superior external attestation.





3. Slaves and Masters (6:5–9)

Paul next addresses the relationship between slaves and masters, the third and final set of household relationships in the household code. As with the other two pairs (wives-husbands, children-parents), Paul first addresses the subordinate member of the slave-master pair, and as with the children-parents pairing, he devotes most of his energy to the subordinate party (Sellin 2008: 465). His advice to slaves consists of a main admonition to obey their masters (6:5a), followed by a series of phrases that describe the quality of this obedience (6:5b–7). Basically, slaves are to perform their duties for their masters with integrity and consider their work as done for Christ. Paul next gives the reason why slaves should do this: God will repay everyone, whether slave or free, for the good they have done (6:8). Surprisingly, he then tells masters to do for their slaves what he has just required slaves to do for their masters (6:9a), and again he finishes with a clause that gives the reason why masters should do this: they too have a master, and he is no respecter of persons (6:9b–c).

Throughout the section the emphasis lies on the leveling effect that Christ’s lordship has on human relationships, and the reciprocity that should result from this among members of the household. Paul achieves this emphasis rhetorically by comparing the lordship of Christ with the lordship of the slave master (6:5, 6, 9b). He achieves it theologically by appealing to the principle of God’s impartiality on the final day of judgment (6:9c).

It is often said that this passage accepts unquestioningly the institution of slavery as it existed in the first century. “There is doubtless no approval, but at the same time no disapproval of the existing slavery in itself,” said Meyer (1880: 318) long ago, and most commentators would agree with him. Some more recent interpreters go further and see in the passage not merely an acceptance of slavery but also an attempt to provide theological support for the institution, particularly as it benefited the slaveholder (e.g., Glancy 2006: 144–45; Harrill 2006: 90–92).

As the notes below explain, however, this passage is more radical than the account of it given in either of these readings. There is no explicit criticism of slavery here, but the level of mutuality and reciprocity that is assumed to exist between master and slave creates an atmosphere in which it would have been difficult for slavery to survive if the advice of the passage had been rigorously followed. The problem that the passage highlights is not its own failure to rise above this brutal and ubiquitous institution, but the failure of those who received the passage as authoritative both in antiquity and in more recent times to live out its radical implications.[1]



Exegesis and Exposition

5Slaves, obey your fleshly masters with fear and trembling in the sincerity of your heart, as to Christ, 6not in mere appearance as people-pleasers but as slaves of Christ, doing the will of God from the inner person, 7working as slaves with goodwill, as for the Lord and not for human beings, 8because you know that each person who does something good will be repaid for this from the Lord, whether slave or free.

9And masters, do the same things for them, with the result that you give up the threat of violence, because you know that their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with him.

[6:5–7] Paul addresses slaves first, just as he has addressed wives and children first in the other two pairs of relationships. Paul’s advice to slaves, like his advice to wives and children, moreover, is that they submit to the authority of the male household head. For wives, the submission is voluntary, but the term used for slaves is identical to the term used for children: they should “obey” their masters. Paul describes the slaves’ “masters” (κύριοι, kyrioi) as “fleshly” (κατὰ σάρκα, kata sarka), and this subtly communicates that there is another “master” (κύριος, kyrios), Christ himself, whose authority is greater than that of any “fleshly” master and to whom the believing slave’s ultimate loyalty lies. Eventually Paul will develop this thought in a direction that, from a theological perspective, levels the ground between slave and master. In 6:9 he reminds believing masters that both they and their slaves have a “Master” (κύριος) in heaven, who is no respecter of persons.

For the moment, however, Paul uses five phrases to describe the slave’s obedience, and each phrase emphasizes the sincerity with which slaves should obey. First, they should obey “with fear and trembling.” Within the NT, this phrase occurs only here and in the undisputed letters of Paul, where it can refer to the Philippian believers’ manner of working out their salvation: they should do so “with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2:12). It can also refer to the Corinthian believers’ willingness to obey Titus when he came to them with corrective advice from Paul: they welcomed Titus “with fear and trembling” (2 Cor. 7:15). In a slight variation of the phrase, Paul says that he came among the Corinthians “in weakness, and in fear, and in much trembling” (1 Cor. 2:3). The phrase, then, seems to refer to the recognition of the subordinate and weak position that one occupies with respect to others. There is nothing here to indicate that the subordinate party fears physical punishment, and insofar as Paul speaks to slaves with believing masters, he makes it clear that he expects masters not to use even the threat of violence against their slaves (6:9). Slaves, then, are to obey in full recognition of the subordinate position they occupy with respect to their masters.

Second, slaves should obey “in ἁπλότητι [haplotēti] of heart.” The term ἁπλότης (haplotēs) means “integrity,” and coupled with “heart” it refers to inner sincerity. It was a virtue highly valued in Hellenistic Judaism (1 Chron. 29:17; Wis. 1:1; T. Reu. 4.1; T. Iss. 3.8; 4.1; 7.7; Ps.-Phoc. 50; Sib. Or. 2.122; cf. BDAG 104; Sellin 2008: 448). In his commentary on Pseudo-Phocylides, W. Wilson (2005: 111) has captured its meaning in these contexts precisely:

As a virtue, it was an important concept of moral anthropology, specifying the personal integrity that accompanies the correspondence of inner feeling with external expression. Predictably, the “soul” or “heart” was identified as the locus of moral efforts intended to cultivate this trait.

In the NT, ἁπλότης is a strictly Pauline word, appearing here, in the parallel passage in Col. 3:22, in 2 Corinthians (1:12; 8:2; 9:11, 13; 11:3), and in Romans (12:8), where it consistently refers to a sincere attitude, often expressed in giving generously to others (Ellicott 1859: 141; BDAG 104). The obedience of the slave, Paul says, should have this straightforward character: there should be no division between the quality of the labor produced and the attitude of the one who produces it.

Third, slaves should obey “as to Christ.” Some early Christian domestic advice urged slaves to “be subject to” their “masters as to a replica of God” (Did. 4.11; cf. Doctrina Apostolorum 4.11), but that is not the meaning here (quoted from Harrill 2006: 88–89). Just as in 6:7 and Col. 3:23, Paul instead contrasts laboring as a slave for human beings with laboring as a slave for the Lord (see the comments above on 5:22). It is not that the master represents Christ to the believing slave, but almost the opposite: the master is factored out of the equation and replaced with the Lord. Work that believing slaves have no choice but to do now becomes a way for them to “walk worthily” of their calling as believers (4:1). In light of this, Harrill’s comment (2006: 90) that masters are the only people in the passage “directly accountable to the Lord” is very wide of the mark.

Fourth, slaves are to obey not merely when the slave master’s eye is on them, as if they were merely to please people, but from their inner being as people who are slaves of Christ and committed to the will of God. The term ὀφθαλμοδουλία (ophthalmodoulia, eye-service) apparently appears here and in Col. 3:22 for the first time in extant Greek literature (as a search of the TLG confirms), but there is little doubt about its meaning, especially since Paul couples it both here and in Col. 3:22 with the term ἀνθρωπάρεσκος (anthrōpareskos, people-pleaser [ESV]). Paul refers to service that is performed only under the gaze of one’s overseer and does not come “from the inner person” (ἐκ ψυχῆς, ek psychēs; cf. the similar contrast in 2 Clem. 13.1).

Once again, Harrill’s comments on the passage misconstrue its meaning. Harrill (2006: 91) argues that the author of Ephesians, in line with ancient optical theory and ideologies of slave control, wanted slaves to identify their masters with the all-seeing Lord, who knew whether the slave was being obedient even in the absence of the earthly master. In addition, slaves must give up any struggle to keep their autonomy and should concede to their masters full power over their inner selves (ψυχαί, psychai).

The Paul of the undisputed letters, however, emphasizes the importance of sincerity and honesty in one’s dealings with others (2 Cor. 1:17–18; 2:17; 3:2; 4:2), a quality that sometimes is translated into specific instructions to those under his authority to obey him “not only in my presence, but now much more in my absence” (Phil. 2:12), or into Paul’s insistence that what he says in his letters when absent he does when he is physically present (2 Cor. 10:11). This ideal of acting sincerely and according to one’s inner convictions was widely valued in ancient Greco-Roman and Hellenistic Jewish ethics, and it is not surprising to see it repeated either in the undisputed letters of Paul with respect to believers generally or in Ephesians and Colossians with respect to the conduct of slaves.[2] It is unlikely, then, to be a subtle power play designed to get more and better work from slaves.

Fifth, Paul says that slaves should do their assigned work “with goodwill” (μετ’ εὐνοίας, met’ eunoias). Ἐυνοία was a virtue that slaveholders valued in a slave. A slaveholder might leave in his will instructions to release at his death his “slave bodies . . . for [their] goodwill [εὔνοιαν] and affection” (P.Oxy. 494.5–6), and another might regret the loss of “the only friendly [εὔνουν, eunoun] and faithful slave she had” (Lucian, Bis acc. 16; trans. Harmon, Kilburn, and MacLeod 1913–67).[3] Slaves should obey their owners, then, with a positive attitude. Perhaps recognizing that this could be difficult because of the innate injustice involved in the institution of slavery, Paul urges slaves to consider their obedience as rendered “to the Lord [κυρίῳ, kyriō]” rather than to human beings.

In sum, slaves should obey their masters with sincerity and integrity, recognizing the subordinate position they occupy. They should avoid a division between the obedience they render and their willingness to render it. Their obedience to their masters (κύριοι, kyrioi) should instead arise from their inner commitment to the Lord (κύριος, kyrios).

[6:8] Paul next gives the reason why the obedience that slaves give their masters should arise from the inner attitude of goodwill he has just described.[4] Any good thing an individual does, he says, is “repaid” by the Lord, and this is true of the slave as much as it is of the free person. The term κομίζω (komizō), when it appears in the middle voice, as it does here, means “receive,” often in the sense of repayment in kind (2 Macc. 8:33; Col. 3:25). Paul uses it this way in 2 Cor. 5:10 to refer to the appearance of believers before Christ’s judgment seat so that “each might be repaid for the things he or she did in the body, whether good [ἀγαθόν, agathon] or not so good [φαῦλον, phaulon].” Although it is possible that the reference here in Ephesians is to the mundane rewards a master might give a slave to encourage the slave’s cooperation and increased productivity (Harrill 2006: 92), it is much more likely, in light of the parallel in 2 Cor. 5:10 and the application of the principle to both “slave” and “free,” that Paul describes the eschatological reward that those will receive whose inner convictions have given rise to good conduct.

The phrase “whether slave or free” (εἴτε δοῦλος εἴτε ἐλεύθερος, eite doulos eite eleutheros) is reminiscent of other statements in the Pauline corpus that nullify social and ethnic divisions for those who have been baptized and who have thus “put on” Christ or the “new human being” (Gal. 3:27–28; 1 Cor. 1:28; 12:13; Col. 3:10–11; cf. Philem. 16). The implication of the statement is clear: ultimately there is no difference between slave and free in God’s eyes. This would come as an encouragement to slaves, whose freedom was often limited merely to the attitude they took toward what they were commanded to do, and it would come as a warning to masters, who may have thought of themselves as free to do whatever they wished with their slaves.

[6:9] Paul now makes this thought explicit as he turns directly to slave masters. The form of his instruction to them is similar to the form of his instruction to slaves, although briefer. Masters are addressed directly (cf. v. 5a); they are instructed in how to behave (cf. vv. 5b–7); and the reason why they should behave this way is given in a clause beginning with the participle εἰδότες (eidotes, because you know; cf. v. 8). Paul can be brief because he intends for masters to act in the same way he has just instructed the slaves to behave—there is no need to repeat himself.

What could Paul mean by saying that masters should “do the same things” to their slaves? Most interpreters claim that Paul merely intends to instruct masters in a general way to treat their slaves as well as their slaves should treat them. The command is another way of urging masters to treat their slaves justly and fairly (Col. 4:1). As Westcott (1906: 90) puts it, there is a presupposition of human equality here, but it is “identity of spirit and not identity of action.”[5] Presumably Paul does not mean that masters should obey their slaves (v. 5), but three considerations make it probable that the radical nature of the statement should not be downplayed.

First, the context moves in the direction of mutuality between slave and master. Paul has spoken of “fleshly masters” in 6:5, subtly reminding slaves and masters alike that they all are ultimately subject to another master. He says this explicitly at the end of 6:8 and the end of 6:9, with his comments that slave and free will be treated in the same way at the final judgment and that there is no favoritism with the heavenly master to whom both are ultimately subject.

Second, there was a strong conviction in early Christianity, originating in the teaching of Jesus, that those in positions of authority should adopt the role of slaves with respect to those under their authority (Mark 10:41–45; Matt. 20:24–28; John 13:1–17; cf. Luke 12:37). The Paul of the undisputed letters was aware of this ethic of mutual service (Gal. 5:13; 1 Cor. 9:19), and it is likely that the mutual submission articulated at the head of the household code, in 5:21, is indebted to it (pace Best 1998: 583).

Third, the theology of Eph. 1–3 is deeply indebted to the notion that human beings are united with one another in their rebellion against God (2:2–3, 11–12; 4:17–19, 22; 5:7–8a) and in the opportunity to become newly created human beings through faith in the gospel (2:10, 14–22; 4:23–24). It is plausible to think of the mutuality expressed in the phrase “do the same things for them” as originating from this view of humanity.[6]

This approach is consistent with Paul’s next step: he deprives masters of the threat of violence (ἀπειλή, apeilē), the primary means of slave control in antiquity.[7] Slaves were regularly beaten with the whip in Roman society, a reminder to everyone of their low social status as people completely without honor (Saller 1994: 133–53). Slave masters could, and regularly did, vent their anger on their slaves with various forms of physical abuse, an activity that was occasionally criticized, but even then, the concern was typically with the harm that excessive wrath might do to the master rather than any feeling of pity for the slave (W. V. Harris 2001: 317–36). Although positive encouragement to obey was also used to keep slaves in submission, violence was the primary foundation of the institution: “Slaves were never in a position to predict when the wrath of an owner would descend upon them and their lives were thus conditioned by this perennial fear of physical abuse and maltreatment. Within that element of fear lay owners’ capacity for the permanent control of their slaves” (Bradley 1987: 137; cf. Garnsey 1996: 8–9; W. V. Harris 2001: 322). Believing masters, however, must “give up” (ἀνίημι, aniēmi) the threat of violence.[8] The command is not qualified in any way. It is not that masters must give up certain forms of threatening (pace Hoehner 2002: 814), but they must give up threatening entirely. With this command, Paul has cut the thread that held the institution of slavery together.

He concludes by providing the reason why masters should act in such countercultural ways toward their slaves: there is no favoritism with the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the “master” (κύριος, kyrios) not only of slaves, but also of slave masters (κύριοι, kyrioi). The principle frequently expressed in the OT and early Judaism that God is an impartial judge (e.g., Deut. 10:17; 2 Chron. 19:7; Sir. 35:12–13; Jub. 5.16; 21.4; 30.16; 33.18; T. Job 43.13) was used in early Christianity to demonstrate the theological legitimacy of the gospel’s reach across ethnic lines from Jews to Gentiles (Rom. 2:11; Acts 10:34–35; cf. Dunn 1988: 89; BDAG 887). Here Paul applies the same principle to differences in social standing, with the effect that there is no difference between slave and master when both are in the presence of the Lord (cf. Gal. 2:6; Col. 3:25).

Summary

In 6:5–9 Paul concludes his advice on how believers within a traditional Greco-Roman household can live wisely, do the Lord’s will, grow in maturity as human beings, and live in the Spirit (5:15–18). Slaves may wonder how any of this can happen for them since they are not free to live as they choose. Paul’s advice shows that these characteristics of the believer’s life can be theirs also since they can always freely choose what their attitude will be to the work they are forced to do. They can view even forced labor as a way of serving the Lord, and this will reduce the tension between their inner disposition toward their work and the work itself. The Lord, moreover, is not really a slave master. He makes no distinction between slave and free, but rewards both groups on the final day not according to their social status but according to the good they have done.

Paul’s advice to believing slave masters subtly undermines the whole system of slaveholding. Slave-owning believers are, in a sense, to submit to their slaves (5:21), serving their slaves in the same way they desire their slaves to serve them. The threat of violence is impossible in such an arrangement, and without the threat of violence, the whole system will theoretically collapse.

This is the only option consistent with the anthropology and soteriology of Eph. 1–3. If every believer had been previously dead because of sin, and if the cross has torn down not only the wall of sin between every believer and God but also the wall between every believing Gentile and Jew (2:14), then the wall between slave and free also has to crumble.





X. Avoiding and Transforming the Deeds of Darkness (5:3–14)

XI. Wise Conduct within the Household (5:15–6:9)

XII. Standing against the Strategies of the Devil (6:10–20)

XIII. A Concluding Commendation and a Final Prayer-Wish (6:21–24)


XII. Standing against the Strategies of the Devil (6:10–20)

Paul concludes the main part of his letter with a stirring call to arms and to prayer in light of all that he has said up to this point. “Henceforth” (τοῦ λοιποῦ, tou loipou; 6:10) his readers should be strong in the mighty strength of God by putting on the armor that God provides and being devoted to constant prayer. Only in this way will they be able to “stand” against the onslaught of the devil and his cosmic allies.

The passage shows the same curious mixture that appears elsewhere in the letter of a clear general structure that is ambiguous in its details.[1] At one level, the passage seems to fall into two sections: an exhortation to be strong, using military imagery (6:10–17), and an exhortation to pray that is more straightforward and in which the military imagery all but disappears (6:18–20).[2] At the grammatical level, however, these two distinct parts are closely tied together. The participles προσευχόμενοι (proseuchomenoi, praying) and ἀγρυπνοῦντες (agrypnountes, watching) at the beginning of the exhortation to pray (6:18) depend grammatically on the imperative δέξασθε (dexasthe, receive) at the end of the exhortation to put on the armor of God: “Receive [δέξασθε] the helmet of salvation and the sword that comes from the Spirit, which is the word of God, praying [προσευχόμενοι] at all times in the Spirit, through every prayer and urgent petition, and being watchful [ἀγρυπνοῦντες] in this very thing with all devotion and urgent petition for all the saints.”

Despite these structural ambiguities, the purpose of the section is clear. It exhorts the letter’s readers, in light of all that has been said, to be strong in the Lord. In 1:17–23, Paul reported to his readers that when he prayed for them, he asked God to enlighten the eyes of their hearts so that they might understand the massive power that God has placed at their disposal through the risen and victorious Christ. This power has given them victory over “the Ruler of the realm of the air” (2:2, 6) and has constituted them as a unified people. Paul can describe this unified people by using the imagery of a newly created “human being” (2:15; cf. 4:11–16) and of the “dwelling place” of God’s Spirit (2:19–22). As a unified church, they are the primary evidence that God’s plan to unite all things in heaven and on earth in Christ (1:9–10) is being successfully executed (3:6), and so the church serves as a witness to the enemy powers of the cosmos that their defeat remains secure (3:10). This critical unity, however, needs to be worked out in practical ways in the day-to-day interaction of believers with each other (4:1–16; 4:20–5:2; 5:15–6:9) and with the unbelieving world (4:17–19; 5:3–14).

With this concluding call to arms and exhortation to pray, Paul draws these themes together and succinctly outlines the task that lies ahead for his readers. God’s great strength is available to them in Christ (1:19–23), but they must be empowered in this great strength (6:10). They have been rescued from following the Course of this world, the Ruler of the realm of the air (2:2), but they must recognize the strategic cleverness of their foe, who is not blood and flesh, and that the enemy’s defeat, although certain, has not yet been accomplished (6:11–12). They know the truth (1:13; 4:21, 24–25; 5:9), understand righteousness (4:24; 5:9), and have been prepared for battle by the gospel of peace (2:14–15, 17; 4:3). They have exercised faith in the gospel (1:13; 2:8; 3:12, 17) and through it have received the Spirit and salvation (1:13; 2:8). Now they must “put on,” “take up,” and “receive” these gifts anew and in the present time (6:11, 13, 14–15, 17). In this way they will be able “to stand” (στῆναι, stēnai; 6:11, 13), “stand” (στῆτε, stētei; 6:14), and “to withstand” (ἀντιστῆναι, antistēnai; 6:13 NRSV) the onslaught of the devil and the cosmic powers aligned with him.

This section of Ephesians has played an important role in the argument that the letter is pseudonymous. It seems to some interpreters to be an edited version of Col. 4:2–4, where there is also a request for prayer whose vocabulary is similar to Eph. 6:18–20.
