It is difficult, say these interpreters, to imagine Paul editing Colossians in this way (e.g., Lincoln 1990: lii; Schnackenburg 1991: 30, 281, 282, 284).[3] The reference to Paul’s coworkers in Col. 4:3 (“praying at the same time for us”), moreover, has dropped away (Schnackenburg 1991: 282–83), and in the view of some interpreters, Paul now appears as a martyr, boldly bearing witness to the gospel despite his imprisonment (e.g., Lincoln 1990: 441; 1995: 109; Sellin 2008: 484–87). Such a portrait seems to fit better in the late first century, when Paul was becoming a legendary hero, than during Paul’s lifetime (Sellin 2008: 58, 486; cf. Beker 1991: 71–72).

This understanding of the paragraph, however, is not convincing. As Muddiman (2001: 295) observes, it is difficult to imagine what would motivate a pseudonymous author to make the minute and seemingly inconsequential adjustments to the vocabulary of Col. 4:2–4 that this theory requires (see footnote 3). Judgments about what seems characteristic of the late first century and what seems characteristic of the historical Paul are subjective, but it does not seem implausible that the Paul of the undisputed letters would speak in the voice of Eph. 6:18–20, asking the Ephesians to pray for him that he might proclaim the mystery of the gospel boldly. In Romans, Paul asks his readers to pray for him personally in light of his impending, difficult mission to Jerusalem (Rom. 15:30–32; pace Best 1998: 607, no coworkers are mentioned). In Philippians, the imprisoned Paul values the Philippians’ prayers and hopes that he might not be ashamed but speak boldly when called on to do so (Phil. 1:19–20). The ironic remark in Eph. 6:20 that he “serves as an enchained ambassador,” moreover, seems fully in step with the paradoxical way Paul speaks of his suffering in 2 Cor. 2:14; 4:7–12; 6:4–9; 11:21–33; 12:7–10; and 13:4.

Lincoln (1995) has emphasized both the stirring nature of the rhetoric of this section and its function as a recapitulation of the major themes of the letter. These two characteristics of the section feature largely in his argument that the author has purposely constructed 6:10–20 as a peroratio, or ἐπίλογος (epilogos), the prescribed concluding element for a speech in the ancient rhetorical handbooks (e.g., Aristotle, Rhet. 3.19; Quintilian, Inst. 6.1). The peroratio was supposed to recapitulate the argument of a speech in a way that made the audience ill disposed toward the speaker’s opponents and well disposed toward the speaker himself. This happens in 6:10–20, argues Lincoln (1995: 107–8), when the author describes the devil in bleak terms (“darkness,” “evil”) and uses the device of pseudonymity to engender sympathy among his readers with Paul, who courageously continues to proclaim the gospel despite his chains.

Lincoln (1995: 110–11) also suggests that 6:10–20 borrows elements from the prebattle speeches that generals gave to their soldiers to encourage them to fight bravely (e.g., Xenophon, Cyr. 1.5.7–14; Thucydides, Pel. War 2.89; Polybius, Hist. 3.63–64; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Ant. rom. 6.6–9; Cassius Dio, Rom. Hist. 38.36–46; 50.16–22, 24–30; Herodian, Hist. Emp. 3.6.1–7).[4] Lincoln’s analysis is helpful in a general sense. There may have been an expectation among many well-educated people in the first century that the final part of a discourse should include a summary of what was said, and that an exhortation to action could end with a succinct emotional appeal. The differences between 6:10–20 and either the peroratio or the general’s speech before battle, however, are notable. This passage recapitulates what has gone before and stirs the emotions in a more subtle way than the handbooks envision for the peroratio (Aristotle, Rhet. 3.19.5–6; Quintilian, Inst. 6.1.1–2, 9–55). It is much shorter, moreover, than the typical prebattle speech in the accounts of the Greek historians, and unlike those speeches, it emphasizes the strength of the opposing enemies (6:12) rather than their weakness (Xenophon, Cyr. 1.5.11; Thucydides, Pel. War 2.89.2, 11; Polybius, Hist. 3.64.5–8; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Ant. rom. 6.7.4; Cassius Dio, Rom. Hist. 50.16.2–3; 50.18.1–4; 50.27.6–7; 50.29; Herodian, Hist. Emp. 3.6.6–7). The picture of Paul at the end, moreover, does not so much call the reader to emulate the courage of a martyred hero as ask for prayer for one who seems afraid that he may not, in his own strength, be able to rise to the challenge of what he knows he must do (6:18).

This final section of the letter’s argument, then, is probably not consciously constructed as a peroratio or prebattle speech, nor is it the product of an admiring follower of Paul. It is instead an expansion of the call to watchfulness, arms, and courage that Paul has used elsewhere near the end of his letters (1 Thess. 5:7–8; 1 Cor. 16:13; Rom. 13:11–14), and a realistic request for prayer in difficult circumstances similar to Rom. 15:30–32.

Here Paul subtly sums up what the readers of the letter must do in order to fulfill their role in God’s plan to unite all things in Christ. They must stand against the devil and his forces on the ground that God has won for them in Christ. To do this they must live in the truth of the gospel, the righteousness that it inculcates, the preparation to battle evil that it brings, and the faith with which they first have believed it. They must constantly receive both salvation and the Spirit’s application of the gospel to their lives. In addition, they must constantly and devotedly pray for themselves, for other Christians, and especially for Paul in his difficult circumstances.





XII. Standing against the Strategies of the Devil (6:10–20)

A. Wearing God’s Protective Armor (6:10–17)

B. Persevering in Watchful Prayer (6:18–20)


A. Wearing God’s Protective Armor (6:10–17)

The exhortation to grow strong in the Lord by putting on his armor can be divided into three parts: an introduction that states the basic concern of the exhortation (v. 10); a general command to put on the armor of God, with reasons why it is necessary to do so (vv. 11–13); and a more-specific exhortation to put on six pieces of armor, each identified with an element of the believer’s existence in the Lord (vv. 14–17).

The basic exhortation (v. 10) is almost a title over the whole section, grammatically unconnected to the rest. Paul wants his readers to make use of the great power that God has placed at their disposal and that, according to 1:17–23, he has prayed they would understand (v. 10).

The general command to put on the armor of God (vv. 11–13) explains specifically how Paul’s readers can carry out the exhortation of 6:10 and why they must carry it out. This subsection of the passage is arranged in four parts, the last two essentially repeating the first two:



A command (to put on God’s armor)

The reason for the command (the enemy is nonphysical and powerful)



A command (to take up God’s armor)

The purpose for the command (to prepare for withstanding present evil)



The redundancy of the subsection emphasizes the gravity of its point: believers must prepare themselves for the intense spiritual struggle they are facing if they are to keep the ground that God has won for them in Christ.

Paul next describes six pieces of armor that his readers should put on (vv. 14–17). Each piece is identified with an element of Christian existence that has played an important part in the rest of the letter: truth (1:13; 4:15, 21–25; 5:9), righteousness (4:24; 5:9; 6:1), gospel preparation (1:13; 2:17; 3:6, 8; 4:11), faith (1:1, 13, 15, 19; 2:8; 3:12, 17; 4:5, 13), and salvation (1:13; 2:5, 8; 5:23). Paul connects putting on the first four pieces of armor closely with the initial imperative “stand, therefore” and presents equipping oneself with this armor as the means by which “standing” firm in the midst of the onslaught of evil becomes possible (vv. 14–16). The flow of thought can be displayed in an overly literal translation laid out in schematic form:

Stand



* * *





by having girded your waist with truth



* * *





by having put on the breastplate of righteousness



* * *





by having shod the feet with the readiness of the gospel of peace



* * *





by having taken up the shield of faith



* * *





The last piece of armor in this set, “the shield of faith,” stands apart from the other three as especially important. Paul’s readers are to take it up “in addition to everything else,” and it has a special purpose: “to snuff out all the ignited missiles of the evil one.”

The last two pieces of armor are connected with a new imperative, “receive” (v. 17). The term emphasizes the gift character of these two pieces, but its imperative mood emphasizes that believers have a role to play in making these gifts effective: they must “receive” them.

The tension between what God has already done for believers and the need for believers to appropriate what he has done for them in their day-to-day existence lies beneath all of 6:10–17. Believers are already saved (2:8) by their faith in the word of God (1:13), and this salvation “is the gift of God” (2:8–9). Yet in order to stand against the devil and his cosmic allies, believers must receive these gifts as armor and wield them in their defense.



Exegesis and Exposition

10⌜Henceforth⌝, grow strong in the Lord and in the might of his strength.

11Put on the armor of God that you might be able to stand against the strategies of the devil, 12because ⌜our⌝ intense struggle is not against blood and flesh but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the world-rulers of this darkness, against the evil spiritual beings in the heavenly places. 13Because of this, take up the full armor of God that you might be able to withstand in the evil day, and having prepared everything, to stand.

14Stand, therefore, having girded your waist with truth, and having put on the breastplate of righteousness, 15and having shod your feet with the ⌜readiness⌝ of the gospel of peace, 16in addition to everything else, having taken up the shield of faith by which you are able to snuff out all the ignited missiles of the evil one. 17And receive the helmet of salvation and the sword that comes from the Spirit, which is the word of God, . . .

[6:10] Most commentators quickly pass over the opening phrase of this new section, and this is entirely appropriate if one thinks either that Paul wrote the accusative-case expression τὸ λοιπόν (to loipon) or that, if he wrote the genitive form τοῦ λοιποῦ (tou loipou), he understood it in the same sense as τὸ λοιπόν.[1] In either case, Paul moves to the concluding section of his letter with the simple expression “Finally. . . .”

This simple reading of τοῦ λοιποῦ, however, is not convincing. As the additional note explains, Paul probably did not write τὸ λοιπόν here but τοῦ λοιποῦ, and τοῦ λοιποῦ does not mean “finally.” It is a short form of the phrase τοῦ λοιποῦ χρόνου (tou loipou chronou) and clearly means “from now on,” “in the time that remains,” “henceforth.”[2] It is best to give τοῦ λοιποῦ its natural meaning, therefore, and to understand it as an introduction to an admonition that outlines what Paul wants his readers to do “from now on” (Westcott 1906: 92; Yoder Neufeld 1997: 109–10; 2002: 292).[3] He is urging them to leave the past behind—perhaps their past attitude of discouragement (3:13) or lingering elements of their existence as unbelievers (2:1–3, 11–13; 4:20–25; 5:8). From this point forward they must actively resist the onslaught of the devil and his minions with the gifts of “armor” that God has given his people (6:11–17) and with prayer (6:18–20).

Near the letter’s beginning Paul has told his readers that he constantly prays for God to give them an understanding of his mighty strength (τὸ κράτος τῆς ἰσχύος αὐτοῦ, to kratos tēs ischyos autou), placed at their disposal in Christ (1:17–23). Here in 6:10 he revisits both the concept of God’s power and the concept that this power is available “in Christ.” Now, however, he moves beyond understanding to action by urging his readers to “grow strong [ἐνδυναμοῦσθε, endynamousthe] in the Lord and in the might of his strength.” The term ἐνδυναμόω means “strengthen” in the active voice, and in the passive voice can mean “be strengthened, empowered” (Ps. 51:9 LXX [52:9 MT; 52:7 Eng.]). It was sometimes used to refer to God’s empowerment of someone for a special task. According to the text of Judg. 6:34 LXX (Vat.), “A spirit of the Lord empowered [ἐνεδυνάμωσεν] Gideon” (NETS); and according to Clement of Rome, “Many women, being strengthened [ἐνδυναμωθεῖσαι] by the grace of God, have performed many manly deeds” (1 Clem. 55.3; Holmes 2007): Judith, for example, killed Holophernes (55.4–6), and Esther delivered her people from destruction (55.6).

The imperative form of the verb here, however, makes it likely that the term, although passive, has an active nuance (cf. BDAG 333). Just as Abraham “grew strong in faith” (ἐνεδυναμώθη τῇ πίστει, enedynamōthē tē pistei) by trusting God to be faithful to his promise despite all appearances to the contrary (Rom. 4:20), and just as Timothy should “grow strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” by imitating the faithfulness of Onesiphorus (2 Tim. 2:1; cf. 2 Tim. 1:16–17), so the readers of Ephesians should “grow strong” in their position in the Lord and in their use of the power God has made available to them by putting on the armor of God.

This certainly does not mean that they “grow strong” by their own efforts alone: as 3:16 makes clear, believers are “strengthened in power” by God, as a free gift. Paul nevertheless considers it also appropriate to call on them to “be strengthened” by making use of the gifts God has given them (“put on,” v. 11; “take up,” v. 13; “stand firm,” v. 14). In a similar way, Paul can urge the Corinthians, “Be watchful, stand firm in the faith, take courage, grow strong [κραταιοῦσθε, krataiousthe]” (1 Cor. 16:13; Bruce 1984: 403).

[6:11] Although no conjunction links this next sentence with what Paul has just said, the logic is straightforward. To be empowered “in the Lord and in the might of his strength” (v. 10), Paul’s readers must “put on [ἐνδύσασθε, endysasthe] the armor [πανοπλίαν, panoplian] of God.” As we saw in the comments on 4:22–24, the metaphor of “putting on” certain ethical qualities as one would put on clothing was common in the OT, Hellenistic Judaism, and Greek philosophy, and in 4:22–24 Paul was concerned that his readers clothe themselves with righteousness, holiness, and truth.

Paul’s use of the metaphor here shares with 4:22–24 the idea that his readers should “put on” a particular set of characteristics, but the metaphor itself moves in a different direction. Here it is closely related to a traditional image, which also appears in Isa. 59:17 and Wis. 5:16–23, of God as an armor-equipped warrior doing battle against injustice.[4] It is unclear whether Paul and the author of Wisdom borrowed their language from Isaiah independently of each other or whether the similarities among the three texts result from a common use of traditional language.[5] In either case, Paul has used the language of God’s armor in his own way. He speaks not of a heavily armed God appearing on the scene to battle injustice but of God’s people putting on the armor that God supplies and defending themselves against the devil.

This shift is not new in the Pauline literature, nor is the picture of the individual battling the values of most of the rest of the world unique to early Christian literature. In 1 Thess. 5:8 Paul can urge believers to stand apart from “the rest” of the world by “putting on [ἐνδυσάμενοι, endysamenoi] the breastplate of faith and love, and as a helmet, the hope of salvation.” In 2 Cor. 10:3–6 he can describe his own ministry among the Corinthians as the work of an army that destroys the philosophical arguments of those who oppose the knowledge of God (cf. 2 Cor. 6:7). In Rom. 13:12 he can tell the Roman believers, “Let us set aside, therefore, the works of darkness, and let us put on the weapons [ἐνδυσώμεθα δὲ τὰ ὅπλα, endysōmetha de ta hopla] of light” (cf. Rom. 6:13). Timothy should fight the good fight (1 Tim. 1:18) and accept suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus (2 Tim. 2:3–4).[6]

Malherbe points out that Seneca (Ep. 96.5; cf. 107.9), writing at roughly the same time as Paul, can speak of life’s difficulties as a battle that the Stoic should fight with courage (cf. Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 3.31–37]). Cynic philosophers, too, thought of the distinctive way of dress that announced their philosophical commitments as armaments against the luxurious life of those who shunned philosophy (e.g., Pseudo-Crates, Ep. 23; Pseudo-Diogenes, Ep. 34).[7] It seems reasonable to think of Paul adopting the language of the OT but perhaps shifting the armor from God to the individual believer in a way that was consistent with the use of the similar metaphor in the philosophical traditions of his time.

If this was his procedure, we should be cautious about reading too much of the broader context of Isa. 59:17 into the meaning of the passage. It is certainly not irrelevant, as the comments below will show, but his meaning is reasonably clear as it stands, and on its own terms. God has given his armor to his people.[8] Like any soldier preparing for battle, his people must put their armor on, and as they do so, they become strong in the mighty power of God (v. 10).[9]

The purpose for doing this is to stand against the “strategies [μεθοδείας, methodeias] of the devil.”[10] They are standing on ground that God’s anointed king, Jesus, has already won for them (1:20–23; 4:8), but they must stand against the devil’s cleverly planned counterinsurgency tactics (Schwindt 2002: 360). As we saw in the comments on 4:14, the rare word μεθοδεία probably means “system,” or in a military context such as this, “strategy” (cf. Best 1998: 592; pace Abbott 1897: 181). The “devil” is identical with “the evil one” in 6:16 who fires ignited missiles at believers. He is the being who in 2:2 is called “the Ruler of the realm of the air” and is said to be powerfully active among unbelievers, who blindly go along with the sinful structures of the world. In 4:27 Paul has told his readers that they need to be alert to the devil’s willingness to take advantage of opportunities, such as anger, to harm believers. Elsewhere in the Pauline corpus, Satan is a plotting, clever adversary (2 Thess. 2:9–10; 2 Cor. 2:11; 11:14), bent on hindering the gospel’s progress (1 Thess. 2:18) and ready to take advantage of any opportunity to lead believers into sin (1 Cor. 7:5) or to inflict pain on them (2 Cor. 12:7).[11] Jerome has captured Paul’s meaning precisely:

Just as wise leaders of armies are accustomed to assault especially those places of a city which are least protected so that, when they have broken in through those places, the protected areas may be easily captured, so also the devil seeks to break in and reach the very citadel of our heart and soul through those places which he sees lying open or perhaps not shut up firmly. (Heine 2002: 254)

When believers put on God’s armor, they protect themselves against this clever enemy.

[6:12] Paul continues to explain why it is necessary to become strong in God’s mighty power with a more-detailed description of both the kind of warfare in which believers are engaged and the opponents against whom they are fighting. First, he says that the warfare in which believers are engaged is an “intense struggle” (πάλη, palē), but “not against blood and flesh.” A πάλη is literally a “wrestling match,” and commentators have frequently wondered why Paul has mixed his metaphors by depicting fully armed soldiers meeting their opponents in an athletic contest that was typically performed in very little, if any, clothing (Gudorf 1998: 331–32). The issue, however, has probably been blown out of proportion. Fully armed conflict had already been described by using the metaphor of an athletic wrestling match in well-known tragedies by Aeschylus (Cho. 866–68) and Euripides (Heracl. 158–61).[12] In addition, Gudorf (1998) has now shown that the best fully armed soldiers were sometimes thought to be expert wrestlers as well. The shift to the terminology of a wrestling match was, therefore, more natural in first-century Greek than it might seem to us.

A wrestling match involves close, intense conflict. By explaining believers’ conflict with the devil and his minions in these terms, Paul emphasizes the gravity of the situation that believers face and the great need for them to put on the full armor he is about to describe.

The enemies with whom believers are locked in combat are not merely the devil (v. 11) but also an array of “evil spiritual beings” (τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας, ta pneumatika tēs ponērias). Paul calls them “spiritual” beings probably because they are related to “the spirit now powerfully working within the sons of disobedience” (2:2) in the same way that “every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (1:3) is related to God’s Spirit (Fee 1994: 28–32). They are as intimately attached to the devil as God’s blessings are to God’s Spirit.

The expression “blood and flesh” (αἷμα καὶ σάρκα, haima kai sarka) emphasizes the weak, mortal nature of humanity, especially in contrast to spiritual beings, such as the gods.[13] The second-century-AD orator Polyaenus (Strat. 3.11.1), for example, claims that the famous Athenian soldier Chabrias told his fellow soldiers before battle, “Since we are about to fight, let us not in any event think that we are engaging the enemy’s gods, but men who have blood and flesh [αἷμα καὶ σάρκας] and who have shared the same nature we do” (3.11.1; trans. Krentz and Wheeler 1994: 1.293; cf. Schweizer, TDNT 7:99). This was meant to encourage the soldiers to believe that they had a chance of winning the battle. Paul’s admonition uses the metaphor “blood and flesh” in a similar way, but his overall point moves in the opposite direction. Without the armor of God, the believer will be unable to prevail against these nonphysical evil beings.

Paul names these formidable foes as ἀρχαί (archai, rulers), ἐξουσίαι (exousiai, authorities), κοσμοκράτορες (kosmokratores, world-rulers), and πνευματικά (pneumatika, spiritual beings). The last name is probably a general term intended to cover any nonhuman evil powers he may have missed (Best 1998: 594). The first two names have already been paired in 1:21 and 3:10, but the term κοσμοκράτωρ appears here for the first time in known Greek literature.[14] When the term shows up in the second and third centuries, it refers first to the planets, which in antiquity were often thought to be fate-controlling deities, then to various gods (Zeus, Sarapis, Helios), and finally to the emperor.

The Testament of Solomon may provide some insight into its meaning despite its late date and Christian redaction.[15] In this text Solomon conjures seven demons, who identify themselves to him as “heavenly bodies, rulers of this world of darkness [κοσμοκράτορες τοῦ σκότους, kosmokratores tou skotous].” The description that follows makes it reasonably clear that these demons are planets. They are larger than the stars, change their positions, and “are named like gods” (T. Sol. 8.2–4; OTP 1:969–70). Five of them describe themselves as vices: deception, strife, fate, distress, and error. The two others simply and ominously call themselves “Power” and “The Worst.” A similar scenario unfolds later in the same work, this time with thirty-six heavenly bodies, “the world rulers of the darkness of this age” (οἱ κοσμοκράτορες τοῦ σκότους τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου, hoi kosmokratores tou skotous tou aiōnos toutou; T. Sol. 18.2; OTP 1:977). The Testament of Solomon may have been influenced by Ephesians, but even so, it probably reflects the kinds of associations Paul intended his reference to κοσμοκράτορες to carry.

Paul’s qualifying phrase, “of this darkness” (τοῦ σκότους τούτου, tou skotous toutou), describes the realm over which these powers hold sway. In Ephesians the concept of “darkness/be darkened” (σκότος/σκοτόομαι, skotos/skotoomai) is associated with alienation from God, ignorance, hard-heartedness, and debauchery (4:18; 5:8, 11–12). The “world rulers of this darkness,” then, are the evil spiritual powers who preside over the chaos that those alienated from God have brought on themselves (2:1–3; 4:17–19).

All the evil powers Paul lists are located “in the heavenly places” (ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις, en tois epouraniois). In Ephesians, “the heavenly places” are the location of the risen, victorious Messiah Jesus (1:20–21); of believers who are “in” him (2:6) and so receive his blessings (1:3); but also, as here, of a host of enemy powers (3:10; W. H. Harris 1991: 89). Since believers live both in the heavenly places (1:3; 2:6) and within the give-and-take of everyday life (4:17–6:9), the phrase refers more to a “dimension” of existence than simply to heaven as opposed to earth.[16] In this spiritual dimension, Christ has already won the victory over the rebellious and demonic powers (1:20–22a), but the victory has not yet been fully implemented. Demonic powers are still active in the world, influencing the “Course” it takes and working within human beings who continue to rebel against the Creator (2:2–3). It is necessary, then, for believers to put on God’s full armor, to take their stand on the ground that Christ has won, and to resist the final, ultimately futile attacks of the devil.[17]

[6:13] The phrase διὰ τοῦτο (dia touto, because of this) refers back to the list of evil spiritual powers: it is necessary to take up the full armor of God because of the strength of the cosmic enemies Paul has just mentioned. Although 6:13 repeats the substance of 6:11, then, there is a slight shift in emphasis. In 6:11 believers need to put on God’s armor because of the shrewdness of the devil’s strategies against them, but here they need to take up the armor because of the power of the devil and his minions who are opposed to them.[18] The battle is against formidable foes who have mounted an attack against ground that the soldier’s king has already won and occupied. The soldier’s duty is to “withstand” (ἀνθίστημι, anthistēmi; NRSV) the onslaught of that enemy and so to remain standing.

It is unclear, however, whether the phrase ἅπαντα κατεργασάμενοι στῆναι (hapanta katergasamenoi stēnai) means that the soldier in the imagery should stand “after preparing everything” or “after winning the victory” (cf. LSJ 924; BDAG 531). The first meaning fits Paul’s normal and frequent use of κατεργάζομαι (katergazomai) elsewhere (do, produce, prepare, perform).[19] The second meaning fits the immediate context of the battle imagery nicely (cf. Herodotus, Hist. 6.2.6; Thucydides, Pel. War 4.85.2) but would give κατεργάζομαι a unique meaning within the Pauline corpus.

The way Paul develops his image of a soldier arming himself for battle tilts the decision in favor of the usual Pauline meaning for the word (cf. Hoehner 2002: 836). His focus throughout 6:10–17 is not on the victory itself (pace, e.g., Chrysostom, Hom. Eph., hom. 22 [NPNF 13:160]) but on the preparations that must be made by taking up the armor of God in order to obtain the victory. This becomes especially clear in the parallelism between 6:13b and 6:14a. The more specific picture in 6:14a of the soldier “standing” (στῆτε, stēte) after girding himself with truth parallels the general picture in 6:13b of the soldier “standing” (στῆναι, stēnai) after making all the necessary preparations for battle. The phrase ἅπαντα κατεργασάμενοι στῆναι, therefore, refers not to a soldier left standing after the battle is over, but to one who has finished “preparing” for battle and is now ready for the attack.[20]

The attack takes place at a particular time: “the evil day.” Paul uses a similar phrase in 5:16, but there the plural makes it clear that he is speaking of the constantly recurring evils of the “times” in which he and his readers live. The singular and definite form of the phrase here has led interpreters to understand it in a wide variety of ways:



The everyday difficulties of living as a marginalized believer in a world dominated by the devil (Theodoret [R. Hill 2001: 2.55]; cf. 5:16)

Particularly difficult experiences of hardship that arise in the course of the believer’s life (Calvin 1965: 219; Eadie 1883: 464–65)

The final day of intense evil prior to the ultimate victory of God, a day for which believers must ready themselves with the armor of God (Meyer 1880: 331)

The final day of evil, but in a “hazy” sense without any clear eschatological overtones (Schnackenburg 1991: 275–76; cf. Best 1998: 596–97)

The final day of evil, which the author of Ephesians believes is now present but not yet in all its fullness (Barth 1974: 804–5; Lincoln 1990: 446; Sellin 2008: 478–79)

This last explanation is probably correct since it represents the basic orientation of the Pauline eschatological tradition, particularly in contexts where Paul urges believers to put on metaphorical armor (1 Thess. 5:8; Rom. 13:12; Best 1998: 596). The “last days” have arrived, and evil has intensified its grip on the world (cf. 1 Tim. 4:1; 2 Tim. 3:1; 4:3; 2 Pet. 3:3; Jude 18). In light of this, and of the strength of their cosmic foes, believers need to take up the armor of God.

[6:14] Paul now begins to describe taking up God’s armor in detail.[21] The point of it all, he says once more, is to “stand” firm (στῆτε, stēte), presumably on the ground that the Messiah Jesus has already gained for the church (1:20–23; 4:8–10).

For this to happen, Paul’s readers must first have “girded” their “waist with truth” (περιζωσάμενοι τὴν ὀσφύν . . . ἐν ἀληθείᾳ, perizōsamenoi tēn osphyn . . . en alētheia). Although Paul does not use the word for “belt” here (cf. 6:15), the verb περιζώννυμι (perizōnnymi, gird) naturally produces the image of a soldier girding his waist with a belt, an important piece of military equipment in both Jewish and Greco-Roman culture. In the Jewish armor described in the OT, the belt held the warrior’s sword (1 Sam. 17:39; 18:4; 25:13; Neh. 4:18 [2 Esd. 14:12 LXX]; Oepke, TDNT 5:305). Roman soldiers also dangled their swords from belts, and sometimes they wore two belts crossed, one for a sword and one for a dagger (Bishop and Coulston 2006: 106).

Paul’s description of the girding of the waist is probably dictated less by any particular piece of military equipment in the armor of the first-century Roman soldier, however, than by the expressions used in Isa. 11:5 LXX. There a descendant of David comes both to God’s people and to the nations to judge them justly and to punish the wicked (11:1–4). “He shall be girded with righteousness around the waist [δικαιοσύνῃ ἐζωσμένος τὴν ὀσφὺν αὐτοῦ, dikaiosynē ezōsmenos tēn osphyn autou] and bound with truth [ἀληθείᾳ, alētheia] around the sides” (11:5 NETS). Both here and in Ephesians, the armored soldier fights evil with virtues that are depicted as pieces of military equipment, and truth is one of those virtues. In the Isaiah text, however, the attack is offensive and is already under way, whereas here in Ephesians the soldier is preparing for an assault on his position, and as part of his preparations, he straps truth around himself.

References to truth elsewhere in Ephesians link it closely with speech (4:25), particularly with the proclamation of the gospel (1:13) and the teaching about Jesus (4:21). It is also closely aligned with “righteousness,” “goodness,” and “holiness” (4:24; 5:9). Since Paul will shortly explain the soldier’s footwear as “the readiness of the gospel of peace” (6:15), he probably has in mind here also the truth of the good news that is centered on Jesus and his reconciling death on the cross (2:14–18). This is the truth that, when lovingly expressed (4:15), will successfully defeat “human trickery . . . in the service of the system [μεθοδείαν, methodeian] of error,” especially insofar as this trickery involves false teaching about Jesus (4:14; cf. 4:20–21). It is easy to think of such trickery in this context as one of the devil’s “strategies” (μεθοδείαι; 6:11).

In order to stand, Paul’s readers must also have “put on the breastplate of righteousness.” The “breastplate” (θώραξ, thōrax) was a metal shield worn like a shirt over the breast to protect the chest (Philo, Alleg. Interp. 3.115) and the vital internal organs located there (Josephus, Ant. 8.414). Soldiers, therefore, “put” it “on” (ἐνδύομαι, endyomai) like a piece of clothing (1 Thess. 5:8; Philo, Embassy 97; Josephus, Ant. 7.283; cf. Isa. 59:17; Wis. 5:18). The first-century Roman “breastplate” consisted of three main parts: a set of horizontal metal strips, joined at the back with hinges and at the front with leather ties or buckles, which covered the midriff; a set of metal plates, again hinged at the back and buckled in the front, which covered the upper chest and back areas; and a set of vertically arranged metal strips that arched over both shoulders and were riveted to the metal plates. This arrangement was flexible when in use, could be disassembled for easy transport, and was more useful than metal mail at absorbing blows. Soldiers probably wore padding under the shoulder area, and they certainly wore scarves around their necks to prevent chafing.[22]

Although this was probably what Paul pictured when he thought of a “breastplate,” he made nothing of its details. His emphasis lies on the identification of the breastplate with “righteousness” (τῆς δικαιοσύνης, tēs dikaiosynēs; a genitive of apposition). His language recalls Isa. 59:17 LXX, where the Lord has endured the injustices of his people against one another long enough, and “appalled that there was no one to intervene” (59:16), he finally comes himself, dressed as a warrior, to “bring wrath to his adversaries” (59:18) and redemption to those willing to turn from their transgression (59:20). “And he put on righteousness like a breastplate [θώρακα, thōraka] and placed a helmet of salvation on his head, and he clothed himself with a garment of vengeance and with his cloak, as one about to render retribution, reproach to his adversaries” (59:17–18a NETS; cf. Wis. 5:18). Just as with the possible allusion to Isa. 11:5 in the soldier’s belt, so here the warrior puts on a particular quality and does battle against evil. Here the correspondence is closer because both the piece of armor and the quality match.

Two differences, however, are also important. First, in Isa. 59:17 the armor aids an offensive attack, whereas here the armor is used to defend a position. Second, in Isa. 59:17 God wears the armor, but here in Ephesians God provides his own armor for his people to wear. The pattern of his allusion to Isa. 59:17 here, then, is identical to the pattern of his allusion to Isa. 11:5 in the preceding phrase. The differences between the imagery in Isaiah and Paul’s use of it here probably mean that he is not providing a commentary on Isa. 11:5 and 59:17 but developing the imagery in his own way.

What is the “righteousness” that guards believers from diabolical assault? It could refer to behaving in an upright way (e.g., Alford 1857: 141; Abbott 1897: 185; Lincoln 1990: 448; Hoehner 2002: 841; BDAG 248) or to “the righteousness that comes through faith, justification” (De Wette 1843: 157; cf. Eadie 1883: 468; Best 1998: 599). Elsewhere in Ephesians, righteousness is aligned with virtues: holiness (ὁσιότης, hosiotēs; 4:24), goodness (ἀγαθωσύνη, agathōsynē), and truth (ἀλήθεια, alētheia; 5:9), and here Paul lists it after “truth” (cf. 2 Cor. 6:6–7). Probably, then, Paul is thinking of an ethical quality—being just, fair, equitable, and generally upright in dealings with others (cf. BDAG 247–48). This sort of righteousness is a characteristic of God’s armor (Isa. 11:5; 59:17; Wis. 5:18), and so it naturally characterizes the people who wear his armor.

[6:15] The participle ὑποδησάμενοι (hypodēsamenoi, having shod), like περιζωσάμενοι (perizōsamenoi; having girded) and ἐνδυσάμενοι (endysamenoi; having put on) in 6:14, modifies the imperative στῆτε (stēte, stand) at the beginning of 6:14. It describes a third means by which believers stand against the forces of the devil “in the [present] evil day.” The reference is to the foot equipment that soldiers wore, perhaps to the heavy combat boots that were standard issue for Roman legionaries and a trademark of the Roman army. They were made from leather, with open sections around the sides of the feet and ankles to allow for ventilation and a comfortable fit. Their soles were made of several layers of leather and equipped with hollow-headed metal studs that provided a firm grip on the soil, allowed for comfortable marching, and could even be used as an offensive weapon.[23]

Spiritual soldiers, Paul says, should also have properly equipped feet. Specifically, they should put on their feet “the readiness of the gospel of peace” (ἑτοιμασία τοῦ εὐαγγελίου τῆς εἰρήνης, hetoimasia tou euangeliou tēs eirēnēs). But what does this mean? At some level there is probably an allusion here to Isa. 52:6–7, where the feet of a messenger (in the LXX, it is God) bring the good news of peace. The conjunction of feet, good news, and peace in both passages make this allusion probable (Robinson 1904: 135; Sellin 2008: 482; pace Best 1998: 600). We can also hear an echo of Isaiah’s prominent theme that in the era of Israel’s restoration, good tidings of peace would be announced from the mountaintops (Isa. 40:9; 52:7; O’Brien 1999: 478).

Still, Paul uses the imagery here in a different way than Isaiah uses it. For Paul, the properly shod soldier does not run to proclaim the gospel (pace Robinson 1904: 135, 215; Sellin 2008: 482), but stands to fight against the evil powers (Best 1998: 600). In this instance, the “gospel of peace” is not a message to be proclaimed, but paradoxically, military equipment used in a raging battle.

The expression probably means, then, that the gospel, whose content is peace, is the source of the metaphorical soldier’s “readiness” (ἑτοιμασία). At the center of the gospel stands the death of Christ on the cross, the peace that this death brings between rebellious humanity and its Creator, and the peace that it brings to the various competing factions within humanity itself (2:11–22). The message of this multifaceted reconciliation is the subject of the church’s proclamation to “the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places” (3:10). Fully embracing the gospel of peace in faith (cf. 1:13), then, is necessary preparation for doing battle with the forces of evil, which stand against the believer and against God’s plan to unite all things in heaven and on earth in Christ (cf. 1:10).

[6:16] The “shield of faith” stands apart from the other pieces of equipment in three ways. First, Paul introduces it with ἐν πᾶσιν (en pasin), a phrase that in this context means “in addition to everything else” (cf. Luke 16:26; Dibelius and Greeven 1953: 99). Although this might be nothing more than a way of dividing the first set of three pieces of armor from the second set (Sellin 2008: 482), it seems more likely that it is intended to emphasize the importance of the shield of faith.

Second, unlike the other pieces of equipment he mentions, Paul specifies a purpose for the shield. It will “snuff out all the ignited missiles of the evil one.” This too has the effect of highlighting the importance of this piece of equipment.

Third, the soldier’s θυρεός (thyreos, shield) was the most prominent part of his equipment in size, and critically important in combat. “Size probably varied, but something approximating to the distance from knee to shoulder may have been usual” (Bishop and Coulston 2006: 92).[24] It was made of sturdily constructed wood laminate with outside edges curving toward the soldier and thus providing some protection from the sides as well as the front. It was covered in leather, rimmed with metal, and had a metal boss on the outside for the protection of the hand that held it (Webster 1985: 126–27; Warry 1980: 191). It was critical to the survival of the soldier in combat, whether from missiles launched from a distance or from the blows of weaponry in close combat (e.g., Josephus, J.W. 6.58, 65, 224).

These three considerations make it difficult to agree with Barth (1974: 771) that nothing indicates the shield as more necessary than the other pieces of armor. The shield stands out among the pieces of armor because “faith,” for which it stands, is fundamentally important to the letter’s theology. Faith in the gospel’s witness to Christ Jesus is the means by which Paul’s readers are saved (2:8; cf. 1:13), have access to God (3:12), and have Christ dwelling in their hearts (3:17). The common faith of Paul’s readers binds them together in unity (4:5, 13).

The shield is particularly useful in extinguishing τὰ βέλη τοῦ πονηροῦ τὰ πεπυρωμένα (ta belē tou ponērou ta pepyrōmena, the ignited missiles of the evil one). The term βέλος (belos) could refer to any projectile used as a weapon—a thunderbolt (Josephus, Ant. 1.203), a javelin (Josephus, J.W. 1.296), something launched from a catapult (Polybius, Hist. 11.11.3), or an arrow (Josephus, J.W. 2.547; MM 108; BDAG 174). Sometimes these missiles were set alight to increase destruction and mayhem among the enemy (e.g., Ps. 7:13 [7:14 LXX, MT]; cf. Thucydides, Pel. War 2.75.5; Diodorus Siculus, Biblio. hist. 20.96.7). Paul and his readers may have had in mind the common picture of the gods, or various demonic powers, striking people with their βέλη (e.g., Herodotus, Hist. 4.79; LSJ 313; Schwindt 2002: 376–79).

Against every form of evil (πάντα, panta) that “the evil one” can fire at the believer, the shield of faith serves as an effective defense. It is the means through which the believer’s salvation, access to God, and relationship with Christ remain secure. It is also the foundation of the church’s unity. It is, then, the ultimate defense against the devil’s strategies.

[6:17] For the next two pieces of armor, Paul begins a new sentence. Rather than continuing to use adverbial participles related to the imperative “stand” (στῆτε, stēte) in 6:14, he formulates a second imperative (δέξασθε, dexasthe) that instructs his readers to “receive” the final pieces of their armor.[25] The first of these pieces is ἡ περικεφαλαία τοῦ σωτηρίου (hē perikephalaia tou sōtēriou, the helmet of salvation). The first-century Roman helmet included a padded metal bowl, a short brow guard, a larger and sometimes flared neck guard, and hinged cheek guards. It protected not only the head but also the neck and shoulders (Bishop and Coulston 2006: 101).

This was probably what Paul and his readers pictured when they thought of a soldier’s helmet, but once again, the Greek text of Isaiah supplied Paul’s wording. Following Isa. 59:17 LXX closely, he has used the adjective σωτήριος as a substantive to mean “salvation” rather than the more common noun σωτηρία (sōtēria), which appears both in 1:13 and in the allusion to Isa. 59:17 in 1 Thess. 5:8. In Isa. 59:17, God will wear the helmet of salvation when he comes as a warrior to intervene on the side of justice and as Redeemer of his people. The “salvation” is redemption of his people from their own sin (Isa. 59:20; Oswalt 1998: 527). In 1 Thess. 5:8 Paul urges the Thessalonian believers to put on “as a helmet the hope of salvation” (περικεφαλαίαν ἐλπίδα σωτηρίας, perikephalaian elpida sōtērias). He is echoing the Isaiah passage to tell his readers that they should arm themselves with the certain hope, whose fulfillment the OT promised, that God would save his people.

Here in Ephesians the allusion to Isaiah’s meaning is more distant (despite the closer verbal correspondence) since Paul views the salvation of God as available to his readers in the present (cf. 2:8–9). This shift is consistent with Paul’s concern in the letter generally that his readers understand the great power God has already exercised on their behalf (1:19–23; 3:18–19) when he saved them as a free gift and seated them alongside the victorious Christ (2:5–9).

He urges his readers, then, to receive salvation not because they do not already have it, but because, although they have it, they need to appropriate it constantly in faith. In the context of first-century Asia Minor, where many people believed that the spiritual forces of the air and the heavens controlled their fate, this might mean reminding themselves that they do not need to fear such powers because of all that God has already done for them in Christ (Arnold 1989: 111; cf. Schwindt 2002: 376–79).

Paul’s readers should also receive τὴν μάχαιραν τοῦ πνεύματος, ὅ ἐστιν ῥῆμα θεοῦ (tēn machairan tou pneumatos, ho estin rhēma theou, the sword that comes from the Spirit, which is the word of God). The term μάχαιρα could be used of a knife short enough to chop fruit but large enough to do serious bodily harm (Josephus, J.W. 1.662; Ant. 17.183; Acts 12:2; 16:27; cf. Herodotus, Hist. 6.75; Demetrius, Eloc. 293), such as in hand-to-hand combat (Herodotus, Hist. 7.225; cf. Mark 14:47). It was standard military equipment (Polybius, Hist. 6.23.6; Acts 16:27; Epictetus [Arrian, Epict. diss. 1.30.7]), and unless we include the soldiers’ boots (see above), is the only offensive weapon in the set of armor that Paul describes.

Paul does not identify the sword with the Spirit, as he has identified the breastplate with righteousness, the shield with faith, and the helmet with salvation, although the genitive construction in each case is the same. If the sword were the Spirit, the result would be both theological and syntactical nonsense: believers would control the Spirit, which would then be identified, confusingly, with the word of God. Since the parallelism among the pieces of armor has already been broken by the introduction of the imperative δέξασθε, it is much better to think of the genitive phrase τοῦ πνεύματος (tou pneumatos) as indicating the source of the sword, just as God is the source of the word in the phrase that follows. The Spirit, then, supplies the sword to the believer (pace Lincoln 1990: 451), and this sword is “the word of God.”[26]

“The word [ῥῆμα, rhēma] of God” has been interpreted primarily in two ways. One set of interpreters believes the phrase refers to a Spirit-inspired word targeted against specific diabolical attacks.[27] If this is correct, Jesus illustrates what the author has in mind when he resists Satan’s temptations in the wilderness by quoting Scripture (Matt. 4:1–11; Luke 4:1–13), including a quotation of Deut. 8:3 LXX, “A human being will not live by bread alone, but by every word [ῥῆμα] that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4).

Another set of interpreters believes that ῥῆμα refers to the gospel.[28] This fits the context, since “the gospel of peace” has just been mentioned (6:15), and the gospel is understood in Ephesians as something verbally proclaimed to the readers (1:13). This understanding of the phrase is also consistent with the NT use of ῥῆμα elsewhere to refer to the gospel (Rom. 10:8, 17–18; 1 Pet. 1:25; Heb. 6:5). In the discussion of ῥῆμα in the comments on 5:26, we saw that there the term probably referred to the gospel, which the readers of Ephesians have heard and believed (1:13), and by which they have therefore been spiritually cleansed. Since that (5:26) is the only other use of the term in Ephesians, and since elsewhere in Paul’s Letters it refers to the gospel, we should probably understand it that way here.

The gospel is closely aligned with “truth,” “salvation,” and “peace” in Ephesians (1:13; 2:17; 6:15, 17), whereas the devil stands behind the ignorance, estrangement from God, and enmity that characterize the rebellious, unbelieving world (2:1–3, 12–13; 4:17–19, 26–27). The gospel, with its proclamation of peace between God and humanity and between warring factions within humanity itself, and with its accompanying implications for day-to-day living in “the righteousness and holiness of the truth” (4:24), is the sword that will successfully answer every attack of the evil one. It does this, however, not merely because it provides reliable information and outlines a sensible way of life but also because it is the word of God and therefore carries with it the effective power of God (Ps. 33:6 MT, Eng. [32:6 LXX]; Rom. 1:16; Heb. 4:12), particularly the power to slay the spiritual enemies of God and his people (Isa. 11:4; 2 Thess. 2:8; cf. Sellin 2008: 484).

Summary

Paul nears the end of his letter with a moving admonition for his readers to leave behind the past with its discouragement and immaturity. The present darkness in which the church lives gives ample proof that there is a battle to be engaged. It is not that new territory remains to be conquered but that what Christ’s victory has secured for the church needs to be defended.

If Paul’s readers are to be prepared for this conflict, they must “put on” and “receive” the armor that God has given them: the truth of the gospel, the sort of righteousness that is demonstrated in justice and equity, the readiness for the battle that the peace of the gospel provides, and most important, the shield of faith. To these should be added the assurance that God has saved them and the gospel truths that the Spirit has made effective in their lives.

If believers are clothed in this armor, Paul assures his readers, they will be able to withstand the final, desperate attempts of the devil and his allies to attack God’s people, and at the end they will remain standing.



Additional Notes

6:10. The term translated here as “henceforth” is τοῦ λοιποῦ in Greek and represents a reading that appears primarily in the Alexandrian tradition (e.g., 𝔓46, א, A, B, I, 33, 81, 1175, 1739). A number of manuscripts from the Western (D, F, G) and Byzantine traditions, but with some Alexandrian support (Ψ), read τὸ λοιπόν at this point. Hoehner (2002: 819n1) concludes that the geographical spread and good character of the manuscripts reading τὸ λοιπόν tilts the decision in its favor, especially since “both readings mean the same thing.”

As the comments on this verse above argue, however, τοῦ λοιποῦ consistently means “henceforth” or “from now on” in the literature and is the less-usual phrase in the Pauline corpus, appearing elsewhere only in Gal. 6:17. Τὸ λοιπόν can mean either “from now on” (1 Cor. 7:29; Heb. 10:13) or “finally” (Phil. 3:1; 4:8). It would not only have been more familiar to scribes copying the Pauline corpus, but would probably also have made better sense to them as the introduction to the moving concluding section that follows. These internal considerations, alongside the solid support of the conservative Alexandrian tradition, make the reading τοῦ λοιποῦ likely, and it is correctly adopted by most recent interpreters of the text.

6:12. The manuscript evidence is nearly evenly divided between ἡμῖν and ὑμῖν, with some Alexandrian manuscripts (א, A, I, 1739) and the majority of the Byzantine tradition supporting ἡμῖν, and other early Alexanian manuscripts (𝔓46, B, Ψ, 1175) and the Western tradition (D, F, G) supporting ὑμῖν. There is a consensus among commentators and textual critics, however, that ἡμῖν is correct since scribes would have been more likely to conform an original ἡμῖν to the second person of the surrounding context than the reverse.

6:15. The LXX sometimes uses ἑτοιμασία with the meaning “foundation, base, place” (2 Esd. 2:68; 3:3 LXX [Ezra 2:68; 3:3 MT, Eng.]; Ps. 88:15 [89:15 MT; 89:14 Eng.]; Zech. 5:11; Dan. 11:7, 20, 21 Theod.; LEH 246). A few interpreters have argued for that meaning here: the gospel of peace provides firm footing for the soldier in his battle against the forces of evil (e.g., Barth 1974: 771, 797–99; Best 1998: 585, 600). This meaning is unique to the LXX, however, and seems to be derived from the thought that a foundation was “preparation” for construction work on the rest of a building. In other words, the notion of “readiness” is still the primary meaning of the word (Meyer 1880: 335).
